children.title: Compact-Domain Attainment
children.top_down_role: Attainment on compact feasible domains.

assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a nonempty compact subset of a topological space \(X\).
\(f:K\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is lower semicontinuous and proper on \(K\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in K}f(x)\neq\varnothing\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Weierstrass attainment for a proper lower-semicontinuous function on a nonempty compact domain
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-real lower-semicontinuous form of compact-domain Weierstrass attainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\) be a nonempty compact subset of a topological space \(X\), and let \(f:K\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and lower semicontinuous. Then \(m:=\inf_{x\in K}f(x)\) is finite from below and there exists \(\bar x\in K\) such that \(f(\bar x)=m\). Equivalently, \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in K}f(x)\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper lower-semicontinuous objective on a nonempty compact feasible domain attains its minimum.
knowledge_statements.title: Compact-Domain Attainment

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem is mathematically precise and fits Compact-Domain Attainment, but no citation with an inspectable locator is supplied. An authoritative source is required before candidate review.

children.title: Sequential-Compactness Attainment
children.top_down_role: Attainment through subsequential compactness of minimizing sequences.

assumptions_latex: \(K\) is nonempty and sequentially compact.
\(f:K\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and sequentially lower semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every minimizing sequence has a subsequence converging to some \(\bar x\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{K}f\).

notation.meaning: A sequence whose objective values approach the infimum

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct subsequence argument for sequentially compact feasible sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential formulation, without assuming that compactness and sequential compactness coincide.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\) be a nonempty sequentially compact space and let \(f:K\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and sequentially lower semicontinuous. If \((x_n)\subset K\) satisfies \(f(x_n)\to m:=\inf_{x\in K}f(x)\), then some subsequence \((x_{n_k})\) converges to a point \(\bar x\in K\). Sequential lower semicontinuity gives \(f(\bar x)\leq\liminf_k f(x_{n_k})=m\), hence \(f(\bar x)=m\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convergent subsequence of any minimizing sequence yields a minimizer when the objective is sequentially lower semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.title: Sequential-Compactness Attainment

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The sequential-compactness theorem and content kind fit the leaf, but the statement includes proof steps and has no cited source. Supply an authoritative locator and restate only the theorem claim.

children.title: Topological Compactness Attainment
children.top_down_role: Attainment in nonmetrizable compactness regimes.

assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a nonempty compact topological space.
\(f:K\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and lower semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A minimizing net has a convergent subnet whose limit belongs to \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{K}f\).

notation.meaning: A net indexed by a directed set

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: net-based compactness and lower-semicontinuity argument
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Net-based attainment suitable for compact spaces that need not be metrizable or sequentially compact.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\) be a nonempty compact topological space and let \(f:K\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and lower semicontinuous. Choose a net \((x_\alpha)\subset K\) with \(f(x_\alpha)\to m:=\inf_{x\in K}f(x)\). Compactness supplies a subnet converging to some \(\bar x\in K\). Lower semicontinuity along convergent nets yields \(f(\bar x)\leq m\), so \(f(\bar x)=m\) and the infimum is attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Topological compactness gives a convergent subnet of a minimizing net, and lower semicontinuity makes its limit a minimizer.
knowledge_statements.title: Topological Compactness Attainment

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The net-based theorem correctly targets nonmetrizable compactness, but the statement contains proof narration and no inspectable citation. Supply an authoritative source and retain only the theorem statement.

children.title: Inf-Compactness
children.top_down_role: Compactness localized to objective lower levels.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a topological space.
\(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is an extended-real-valued function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is inf-compact exactly when \(\{x\in X:f(x)\leq\alpha\}\) is compact for every \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\).

notation.meaning: Lower level set at height alpha

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard global definition of an inf-compact function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global inf-compactness; relative inf-compactness on a feasible subset is not included.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a topological space \(X\), a function \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is called inf-compact if, for every real number \(\alpha\), its lower level set \(L_\alpha(f):=\{x\in X:f(x)\leq\alpha\}\) is compact in \(X\). Empty lower level sets count as compact. If \(f\) is proper and bounded below, any nonempty lower level set above \(\inf_X f\) localizes every sufficiently accurate minimizing sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An objective is inf-compact when each of its finite lower level sets is compact.
knowledge_statements.title: Inf-Compactness

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The core definition fits Inf-Compactness, but no terminology source is cited and the final sentence adds a vaguely quantified minimizing-sequence consequence. A sourced replacement should state the definition separately and quantify any additional property precisely.

children.title: Growth Compactness Criteria
children.top_down_role: Growth-based control of minimizing sequences.

children.title: Level-Boundedness Criteria
children.top_down_role: Sublevel-set control of minimizing sequences.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is level-bounded if and only if \(\{x\in\mathbb R^n:f(x)\leq\alpha\}\) is bounded for every \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\).

notation.meaning: Lower level set at height alpha

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional global level-boundedness and its sequential escape characterization.

source_refs.locator: 9.1.5 Boundedness of level sets p. 826
source_refs.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A proper function \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is level-bounded if \(L_\alpha(f):=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:f(x)\leq\alpha\}\) is bounded for every \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\). Equivalently, for every sequence \((x_k)\subset\mathbb R^n\) satisfying \(\|x_k\|\to\infty\), one has \(f(x_k)\to+\infty\). If \(f\) is also lower semicontinuous, every \(L_\alpha(f)\) is compact.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Level-boundedness means every real lower level set is bounded; equivalently, the objective tends to positive infinity along every sequence escaping to infinity. In finite dimensions, lower semicontinuity then makes the lower level sets compact.
knowledge_statements.title: Level-Boundedness Criteria

source_witnesses.locator: 9.1.5 Boundedness of level sets p. 826
source_witnesses.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. II

children.title: Coercivity Regimes
children.top_down_role: Growth conditions preventing escape to infinity.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a normed space.
\(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Coercivity means \(\|x_k\|\to\infty\Rightarrow f(x_k)\to+\infty\), equivalently every lower level set \(\{x\in X:f(x)\leq\alpha\}\), \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\), is norm-bounded.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard norm-coercivity criterion and bounded-sublevel equivalence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Norm-coercivity, distinct from stronger growth rates such as supercoercivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A proper function \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) on a normed space is coercive if, for every sequence \((x_k)\subset X\), \(\|x_k\|\to\infty\) implies \(f(x_k)\to+\infty\). This is equivalent to norm-boundedness of every lower level set \(\{x\in X:f(x)\leq\alpha\}\), where \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\). In finite dimensions, if \(f\) is also lower semicontinuous, these lower level sets are compact.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A norm-coercive objective diverges to positive infinity along every sequence escaping in norm, equivalently every real lower level set is norm-bounded.
knowledge_statements.title: Coercivity Regimes

children.title: Equivalence Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Settings where the two growth conditions coincide or separate.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space.
\(f:H\to\mathbb R\) is given by \(f(x)=\|x\|^2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is coercive and weakly inf-compact, but it is not inf-compact in the norm topology.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: closed bounded balls are noncompact in infinite-dimensional normed spaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shows where coercivity ceases to imply norm-topological inf-compactness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space and define \(f(x):=\|x\|^2\). Then \(f\) is continuous, proper, and coercive, and its lower level sets are closed and norm-bounded. However, \(L_1(f)=\{x\in H:\|x\|\leq1\}\) is not norm-compact, so \(f\) is not inf-compact for the norm topology. Because \(H\) is reflexive, the same level set is weakly compact; thus compactness depends essentially on the chosen topology.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In infinite dimensions, coercivity gives bounded sublevels but not norm-compact ones; weak compactness may still survive.
knowledge_statements.title: Equivalence Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Hilbert-space example is a correct failure boundary separating coercivity from norm-topological inf-compactness, and its content kind fits the leaf. No inspectable source locator is supplied.

children.title: Asymptotic Escape Criteria
children.top_down_role: Asymptotic tests for boundedness and escape directions.

children.title: Horizon Criteria
children.top_down_role: Asymptotic geometry expressed through horizon objects.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and lower semicontinuous.
\(f^\infty\) denotes the horizon function of \(f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is level-bounded if and only if \(f^\infty(d)>0\) for every \(d\neq0\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: finite-dimensional horizon-function characterization of level-boundedness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional horizon-function criterion using the epigraphical horizon construction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and lower semicontinuous, and let \(f^\infty\) be the function whose epigraph is the horizon cone of \(\operatorname{epi}f\). Then \(f\) is level-bounded if and only if \(f^\infty(d)>0\) for every \(d\in\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}\). Equivalently, the zero sublevel of the horizon function satisfies \(\{d:f^\infty(d)\leq0\}=\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper lower-semicontinuous finite-dimensional objective is level-bounded exactly when every nonzero horizon direction has positive horizon value.
knowledge_statements.title: Horizon Criteria

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition has the expected finite-dimensional horizon-function form, but its validity depends on the precise epigraphical horizon definition. No source or exact theorem locator is supplied, so the mathematical version cannot be confirmed reliably.

children.title: Recession Criteria
children.top_down_role: Escape directions detected through recession behavior.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
\(f^{0+}\) is the recession function of \(f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is level-bounded if and only if \(f^{0+}(d)>0\) for every \(d\neq0\).

notation.meaning: A point in the effective domain

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: recession-function characterization for proper closed convex functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed convex finite-dimensional specialization of the horizon criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex. For any \(x_0\in\operatorname{dom}f\), define \(f^{0+}(d):=\sup_{t>0}[f(x_0+td)-f(x_0)]/t\); this value is independent of \(x_0\). Then \(f\) is level-bounded if and only if \(f^{0+}(d)>0\) for every \(d\neq0\), equivalently \(\{d:f^{0+}(d)\leq0\}=\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a proper closed convex function, level-boundedness is equivalent to strictly positive recession cost in every nonzero direction.
knowledge_statements.title: Recession Criteria

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The closed convex recession criterion fits the leaf, but the base-point-independent formula and strict-positivity equivalence require an authoritative definition and theorem locator. None is supplied.

children.title: Asymptotic Escape Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Regimes where nontrivial escape directions obstruct boundedness.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R\) is defined by \(f(x,y)=x^2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) attains its minimum although \(f^\infty(0,1)=0\) and its lower level sets are unbounded.

notation.meaning: Quadratic objective constant in the second coordinate

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: explicit convex counterexample separating attainment from level-boundedness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A nonpositive asymptotic direction obstructs level-boundedness, but does not by itself obstruct attainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(f:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R\) by \(f(x,y):=x^2\). The function is proper, continuous, and convex, and \(\operatorname*{argmin}f=\{(0,y):y\in\mathbb R\}\), so its minimum is attained. Nevertheless, every nonempty lower level set contains the line \(\{(0,y):y\in\mathbb R\}\), and \(f^\infty(0,1)=0\). Thus failure of the strict horizon or recession criterion proves non-level-boundedness, not necessarily nonattainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A zero-cost escape direction can make sublevels unbounded while a whole affine set of minimizers still exists.
knowledge_statements.title: Asymptotic Escape Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The example correctly shows that attainment does not imply level-boundedness and the failure_boundary kind fits the leaf. It lacks a citation with an inspectable locator.

children.title: Compactness Routes for Minimizing Sequences
children.top_down_role: Function-space compactness regimes used in direct-method arguments.

children.title: Weak-Compactness Routes
children.top_down_role: Weak sequential compactness in reflexive and related spaces.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a reflexive Banach space and \(C\subset X\) is nonempty and weakly closed.
\(f:C\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, weakly lower semicontinuous, and norm-coercive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x)\neq\varnothing\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: reflexive-space direct method using weak sequential compactness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reflexive Banach-space direct method based on bounded minimizing sequences and weak lower semicontinuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a reflexive Banach space, let \(C\subset X\) be nonempty and weakly closed, and let \(f:C\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, weakly lower semicontinuous, and norm-coercive. Every minimizing sequence \((x_k)\subset C\) is norm-bounded and therefore has a weakly convergent subsequence \(x_{k_j}\rightharpoonup\bar x\). Weak closedness gives \(\bar x\in C\), and weak lower semicontinuity gives \(f(\bar x)=\inf_{x\in C}f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a reflexive Banach space, coercivity bounds minimizing sequences and weak lower semicontinuity turns a weak cluster point into a minimizer.
knowledge_statements.title: Weak-Compactness Routes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The reflexive-space direct-method theorem fits Weak-Compactness Routes and its hypotheses are sufficient, but the statement contains proof narration and no authoritative citation. Supply a locator and restate only the theorem claim.

children.title: Weak-Star Compactness Routes
children.top_down_role: Weak-star compactness in dual and measure spaces.

assumptions_latex: \(E\) is a normed space and \(C\subset E^*\) is nonempty and weak-star closed.
\(f:C\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, weak-star lower semicontinuous, and norm-coercive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x^*\in C}f(x^*)\neq\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: Continuous dual of the predual space

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Banach-Alaoglu direct method using minimizing nets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual-space direct method using weak-star compact dual balls and nets; no separability assumption is imposed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) be a normed space, let \(C\subset E^*\) be nonempty and weak-star closed, and let \(f:C\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, weak-star lower semicontinuous, and norm-coercive. Then there exists \(\bar x^*\in C\) such that \(f(\bar x^*)=\inf_{x^*\in C}f(x^*)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper, norm-coercive, weak-star lower-semicontinuous objective on a nonempty weak-star closed subset of a dual space attains its minimum.
knowledge_statements.title: Weak-Star Compactness Routes

children.title: Compact-Embedding Routes
children.top_down_role: Compact embeddings and stronger-convergence recovery.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a reflexive Banach space, \(Y\) is a Banach space, and \(J:X\to Y\) is a compact continuous embedding.
The minimizing sequence \((u_n)\subset A\subset X\) is bounded in \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exist \(u\in X\) and a subsequence \((u_{n_k})\) such that \(u_{n_k}\rightharpoonup u\) in \(X\) and \(Ju_{n_k}\to Ju\) in \(Y\).

notation.meaning: compact embedding from the coercive space into the strong-convergence space

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: compact embeddings convert bounded weakly convergent subsequences into strongly convergent embedded subsequences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reflexive-domain compact-embedding route used by the direct method.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be reflexive, let \(Y\) be a Banach space, and let \(J:X\to Y\) be linear, continuous, injective, and compact. Every bounded sequence \((u_n)\subset X\) has a subsequence and some \(u\in X\) for which \(u_{n_k}\rightharpoonup u\) in \(X\) and \(Ju_{n_k}\to Ju\) in \(Y\). Consequently, any constraint and objective term stable under strong convergence in \(Y\) may be passed to the limit along that subsequence, provided the remaining feasibility conditions are weakly closed in \(X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A compact embedding upgrades a bounded sequence's weakly convergent subsequence to strong convergence in the embedded space, enabling limit passage in strongly stable terms.
knowledge_statements.title: Compact-Embedding Routes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The compact-embedding principle and content kind fit the leaf, but no citation or inspectable locator supports the stated theorem and its broad limit-passage consequence.

children.title: Measure Compactness Regime Family
children.top_down_role: Compactness for probability, measure, and concentration-sensitive models.

children.title: Tightness Criteria
children.top_down_role: Uniform control of mass outside compact regions.

assumptions_latex: \(S\) is a Polish space and \(\mathcal M\) is a family of finite nonnegative Borel measures on \(S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal M\) is tight exactly when \(\forall\varepsilon>0\;\exists K_\varepsilon\subset S\text{ compact}:\sup_{\mu\in\mathcal M}\mu(S\setminus K_\varepsilon)<\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: family of finite nonnegative Borel measures

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: uniform tightness is the standard compact-containment criterion for finite measures on Polish spaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform tightness for finite nonnegative measures on a Polish space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A family \(\mathcal M\) of finite nonnegative Borel measures on a Polish space \(S\) is uniformly tight if and only if, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exists a compact set \(K_\varepsilon\subset S\) such that \(\sup_{\mu\in\mathcal M}\mu(S\setminus K_\varepsilon)<\varepsilon\). For probability measures this condition says that one compact set contains at least \(1-\varepsilon\) mass for every member of \(\mathcal M\). For general finite measures, uniform boundedness of \(\mu(S)\) is additionally required in the usual relative-compactness criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform tightness means that, to any tolerance, one compact set captures all but that tolerance of every measure's mass.
knowledge_statements.title: Tightness Criteria

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition correctly states uniform tightness for finite nonnegative measures and fits the leaf, but it has no cited authoritative source or locator.

children.title: Weak Measure Compactness
children.top_down_role: Sequential compactness routes for finite or probability measures.

assumptions_latex: \(S\) is a Polish space and \((\mu_n)\) is a sequence of finite nonnegative Borel measures.
\(\sup_n\mu_n(S)<\infty\) and \((\mu_n)\) is uniformly tight.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exist a finite nonnegative Borel measure \(\mu\) and a subsequence satisfying \(\int_S f\,d\mu_{n_k}\to\int_S f\,d\mu\) for every \(f\in C_b(S)\).

notation.meaning: bounded continuous real-valued functions on the state space

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: this is the sequential finite-measure form of Prokhorov compactness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential Prokhorov compactness for uniformly bounded finite measures.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be Polish and let \((\mu_n)\) be finite nonnegative Borel measures satisfying \(\sup_n\mu_n(S)<\infty\). If \((\mu_n)\) is uniformly tight, then there are a subsequence \((\mu_{n_k})\) and a finite nonnegative Borel measure \(\mu\) such that \(\mu_{n_k}\Rightarrow\mu\); explicitly, \(\int_S f\,d\mu_{n_k}\to\int_S f\,d\mu\) for every \(f\in C_b(S)\). Conversely, every relatively compact family for this narrow topology is uniformly tight and has uniformly bounded total mass.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniformly bounded, uniformly tight finite measures on a Polish space have a narrowly convergent subsequence; relative narrow compactness also forces these conditions.
knowledge_statements.title: Weak Measure Compactness

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem is the appropriate finite-measure form of Prokhorov compactness, but both directions require an authoritative citation with a specific locator.

children.title: Concentration-Sensitive Compactness
children.top_down_role: Compactness regimes accounting for concentrating mass.

assumptions_latex: \((\mu_n)\) is a sequence of Borel probability measures on \(\mathbb R^d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: After subselection, exactly one regime occurs: vanishing, tightness modulo translations, or dichotomy into asymptotically separated masses \(\alpha\) and \(1-\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concentration-compactness trichotomy for probability measures on Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For Borel probability measures \((\mu_n)\) on \(\mathbb R^d\), define \(Q_n(R)=\sup_{y\in\mathbb R^d}\mu_n(B_R(y))\). After passing to a subsequence, the concentration functions determine \(\alpha\in[0,1]\) and one of three regimes: if \(\alpha=0\), mass vanishes uniformly on every fixed-radius ball; if \(\alpha=1\), translations \((y_n)\) exist for which the translated measures are tight; if \(0<\alpha<1\), the measures admit, up to arbitrarily small remainder, components of masses approaching \(\alpha\) and \(1-\alpha\) whose supports become mutually separated.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A probability-measure sequence either vanishes locally, becomes tight after translation, or splits into two positive masses moving arbitrarily far apart.
knowledge_statements.title: Concentration-Sensitive Compactness

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The concentration-compactness role fits the leaf, but the precise trichotomy and dichotomy decomposition cannot be validated without a theorem-level source.

children.title: Mass-Escape Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Loss of compactness through spatial escape or concentration.

assumptions_latex: For \(n\in\mathbb N\), let \(\mu_n=\delta_n\) be the Dirac probability measure at \(n\) on \(\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\mu_n)\) is not tight and has no narrowly convergent subsequence in \(\mathcal P(\mathbb R)\), although \(\int f\,d\mu_n\to0\) for every \(f\in C_c(\mathbb R)\).

notation.meaning: Dirac probability measure at the point n

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: translating Dirac masses are the canonical mass-escape example
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical loss of probability mass at spatial infinity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mu_n=\delta_n\) on \(\mathbb R\). For every compact \(K\subset\mathbb R\), one has \(\mu_n(K)=0\) for all sufficiently large \(n\); hence \((\mu_n)\) is not tight. It therefore has no narrowly convergent subsequence in the probability space \(\mathcal P(\mathbb R)\). Nevertheless, \(\int_{\mathbb R}f\,d\mu_n=f(n)\to0\) for every \(f\in C_c(\mathbb R)\), so \(\mu_n\) converges vaguely to the zero measure. Thus vague convergence can lose total mass when tightness is absent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dirac masses moving to infinity converge vaguely to zero but have no narrow probability limit, showing precisely how failure of tightness permits mass escape.
knowledge_statements.title: Mass-Escape Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The translating-Dirac example is mathematically correct and the failure-boundary kind is appropriate, but no inspectable source is cited.

children.title: Limit-Feasibility Closure System
children.top_down_role: Closure mechanisms for retaining admissibility under the selected convergence.

children.title: Strongly Closed Admissible Classes
children.top_down_role: Closure in norm and metric topologies.

knowledge_statements.title: Strongly Closed Admissible Classes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential characterization of strong closedness in metric spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((X,d)\) be a metric space. An admissible class \(A\subset X\) is strongly closed if it is closed in the topology induced by \(d\). Equivalently, whenever \((x_n)\subset A\) and \(d(x_n,x)\to0\) for some \(x\in X\), one has \(x\in A\). In a normed space this criterion uses \(d(x,y)=\lVert x-y\rVert\). Hence strong closedness is sufficient to ensure that every strongly convergent minimizing subsequence in \(A\) has a feasible limit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An admissible class is strongly closed when every norm- or metric-convergent sequence of feasible points has a feasible limit; this guarantees feasibility of strongly obtained limits.
assumptions_latex: \((X,d)\) is a metric space and \(A\subset X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\) is strongly closed exactly when \(x_n\in A\) and \(d(x_n,x)\to0\) imply \(x\in A\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: sequential closedness equals closedness in metric spaces

children.title: Weak-Topology Closure Pair
children.top_down_role: Closure compatible with weak compactness routes.

children.title: Weakly Closed Admissible Classes
children.top_down_role: Admissible classes preserved under weak convergence.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a Banach space and \(A\subset X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\) is weakly sequentially closed exactly when \(x_n\in A\) and \(x_n\rightharpoonup x\) imply \(x\in A\).

notation.meaning: weak convergence in the Banach space
continuous dual of the Banach space

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential weak closedness, the form used for minimizing sequences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a Banach space. An admissible class \(A\subset X\) is weakly sequentially closed if every sequence \((x_n)\subset A\) satisfying \(x_n\rightharpoonup x\) has \(x\in A\), where weak convergence means \(x^*(x_n)\to x^*(x)\) for every \(x^*\in X^*\). If \(A\) is closed in the full weak topology, then it is weakly sequentially closed. The converse requires additional hypotheses and is not part of this definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A class is weakly sequentially closed when weak limits of feasible sequences remain feasible; full weak closedness always implies this sequential property.
knowledge_statements.title: Weakly Closed Admissible Classes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record correctly defines sequential weak closedness and distinguishes it from full weak closedness, but the terminology and distinction lack an inspectable citation.

children.title: Weak-Star Closed Admissible Classes
children.top_down_role: Admissible classes preserved under weak-star convergence.

assumptions_latex: \(X=E^*\) is a dual Banach space with a specified predual \(E\), and \(A\subset X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\) is weak-star sequentially closed exactly when \(x_n\in A\) and \(x_n\overset{*}{\rightharpoonup}x\) imply \(x\in A\).

notation.meaning: dual Banach space with predual E
weak-star convergence induced by the predual

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential weak-star closedness relative to a fixed predual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=E^*\) be a dual Banach space with specified predual \(E\). An admissible class \(A\subset X\) is weak-star sequentially closed if \((x_n)\subset A\) and \(x_n\overset{*}{\rightharpoonup}x\) imply \(x\in A\), where weak-star convergence means \(\langle x_n,e\rangle\to\langle x,e\rangle\) for every \(e\in E\). Closure in the full weak-star topology implies this property; the converse generally needs metrizability or another sequentiality assumption on the relevant bounded set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relative to a fixed predual, weak-star sequential closedness means every weak-star limit of a feasible sequence is feasible.
knowledge_statements.title: Weak-Star Closed Admissible Classes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The predual-relative sequential definition and warning about full weak-star closure are appropriate, but no authoritative source with a specific locator is provided.

children.title: Closure-Topology Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Alignment between admissible-set closure and the selected compactness topology.

assumptions_latex: \(A\subset X\), and the compactness argument produces convergence in a topology \(\tau\) on \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Limit feasibility is guaranteed when \(A\) is \(\tau\)-sequentially closed; closure only in a strictly finer topology is insufficient in general.

notation.meaning: topology delivered by the compactness argument

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct-method feasibility requires closedness for the convergence topology actually obtained
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatibility condition between subsequential convergence and admissible-set closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a compactness argument yields \(x_{n_k}\to x\) in a topology \(\tau\) on \(X\), with \(x_{n_k}\in A\). The closure hypothesis compatible with that argument is \(\tau\)-sequential closedness of \(A\), namely \(x_{n_k}\in A\) and \(x_{n_k}\to x\) in \(\tau\) imply \(x\in A\). Closure in a topology strictly finer than \(\tau\) does not generally suffice. In particular, norm closedness alone need not preserve feasibility under weak or weak-star convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The admissible class must be closed for the topology in which compactness supplies a limit; closure only in a stronger topology may fail.
knowledge_statements.title: Closure-Topology Compatibility

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The topology-compatibility condition is mathematically sound and fits the leaf, but it lacks cited support.

children.title: Constraint Preservation under Limits
children.top_down_role: Limit stability of pointwise, integral, differential, and boundary constraints.

knowledge_statements.title: Constraint Preservation under Limits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract sequential criterion covering multiple constraint types.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((X,\tau)\) be a topological space, let \(I\) be an index set, and, for every \(i\in I\), let \(Y_i\) be a topological space, \(G_i:X\to Y_i\), and \(C_i\subset Y_i\) be sequentially closed. Assume that, for each \(i\in I\), whenever \(x_n\to x\) in \(\tau\) and \(G_i(x_n)\in C_i\) for all \(n\), one has \(G_i(x_n)\to G_i(x)\) in \(Y_i\). Then \(A=\bigcap_{i\in I}G_i^{-1}(C_i)\) is \(\tau\)-sequentially closed. Pointwise, integral, differential, and boundary constraints fit this principle once the corresponding limit-passage property is established.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A family of constraints is preserved under a chosen sequential limit when every defining quantity converges in its specified target topology and every allowed target set is sequentially closed.
assumptions_latex: \((X,\tau)\) is a topological space and \(I\) is an index set.
For every \(i\in I\), \(Y_i\) is a topological space, \(G_i:X\to Y_i\), and \(C_i\subset Y_i\) is sequentially closed.
For every \(i\in I\), if \(x_n\to x\) in \(\tau\) and \(G_i(x_n)\in C_i\) for all \(n\), then \(G_i(x_n)\to G_i(x)\) in \(Y_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The feasible class \(A=\bigcap_{i\in I}G_i^{-1}(C_i)\) is \(\tau\)-sequentially closed.

notation.meaning: constraint maps into topological target spaces

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: constraints are preserved when their defining maps pass to the chosen limit and their target sets are sequentially closed

children.top_down_role: Topological and integrand-structural routes for objective passage to limits.

children.title: Strong Lower Semicontinuity
children.top_down_role: Lower-semicontinuity in norm and metric topologies.

assumptions_latex: \((X,d)\) is a metric space and \(F:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is strongly lower semicontinuous exactly when \(x_n\to x\) implies \(F(x)\le\liminf_{n\to\infty}F(x_n)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: sequential lower semicontinuity characterizes lower semicontinuity in metric spaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential lower semicontinuity for the metric or norm topology.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((X,d)\) be a metric space and let \(F:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\). The functional \(F\) is strongly lower semicontinuous if, for every sequence \((x_n)\subset X\) with \(d(x_n,x)\to0\), one has \(F(x)\le\liminf_{n\to\infty}F(x_n)\). Equivalently in a metric space, every sublevel set \(\{x\in X:F(x)\le c\}\) is strongly closed for each \(c\in\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A functional is strongly lower semicontinuous when its value at every metric limit does not exceed the limiting lower values along the sequence.
knowledge_statements.title: Strong Lower Semicontinuity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The metric sequential definition and sublevel-set characterization are correct and the definition kind fits, but no authoritative citation is supplied.

children.title: Weak-Topology Lower-Semicontinuity Pair
children.top_down_role: Lower-semicontinuity compatible with weak compactness.

children.title: Weak Lower Semicontinuity
children.top_down_role: Lower-semicontinuity routes for weakly convergent sequences or nets.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a Banach space and \(F:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is weakly sequentially lower semicontinuous exactly when \(x_n\rightharpoonup x\) implies \(F(x)\le\liminf_{n\to\infty}F(x_n)\).

notation.meaning: weak convergence in the Banach space

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential weak lower semicontinuity used in the direct method.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a Banach space and let \(F:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\). The functional \(F\) is weakly sequentially lower semicontinuous if every weakly convergent sequence \(x_n\rightharpoonup x\) satisfies \(F(x)\le\liminf_{n\to\infty}F(x_n)\). Lower semicontinuity for the full weak topology implies this sequential property. Moreover, weak sequential lower semicontinuity implies strong sequential lower semicontinuity because norm convergence implies weak convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A functional is weakly sequentially lower semicontinuous when its value at a weak limit is no greater than the sequence's limiting lower values.
knowledge_statements.title: Weak Lower Semicontinuity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The sequential weak lower-semicontinuity definition and its distinction from full weak-topological lower semicontinuity are correct, but they lack an inspectable source.

children.title: Weak-Star Lower Semicontinuity
children.top_down_role: Lower-semicontinuity routes in dual-space weak-star topologies.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a Banach space with dual \(X^*\).
\(F:X^*\to(-\infty,+\infty]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is weak-star lower semicontinuous exactly when \(x_\alpha^*\overset{*}{\rightharpoonup}x^*\) implies \(F(x^*)\leq\liminf_\alpha F(x_\alpha^*)\).

notation.meaning: weak-star convergence in the dual space

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard net characterization of lower semicontinuity in the weak-star topology
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Topological, net-based definition; sequential formulations require additional metrizability or compactness hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The functional \(F\) is weak-star lower semicontinuous if every net \((x_\alpha^*)\subset X^*\) satisfying \(x_\alpha^*\overset{*}{\rightharpoonup}x^*\) obeys \[F(x^*)\leq\liminf_\alpha F(x_\alpha^*).\] Equivalently, each sublevel set \(\{x^*\in X^*:F(x^*)\leq c\}\) is closed in \(\sigma(X^*,X)\) for every \(c\in\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weak-star lower semicontinuity means that functional values at weak-star limits do not exceed the liminf of values along convergent nets.
knowledge_statements.title: Weak-Star Lower Semicontinuity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The net and sublevel-set characterizations are mathematically appropriate for weak-star lower semicontinuity, and the definition content kind fits the leaf. No inspectable source with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Topology-Compatibility Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Dependence of lower semicontinuity on the chosen convergence topology.

assumptions_latex: \(X=\ell^2\) carries its weak topology.
\((e_n)\) is the standard orthonormal sequence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Norm continuity does not imply weak lower semicontinuity: \(e_n\rightharpoonup0\) but \(F(0)>\liminf_nF(e_n)\).

notation.meaning: the norm-continuous functional used in the counterexample

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: explicit Hilbert-space counterexample separates norm continuity from weak lower semicontinuity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete boundary between strong-topology continuity and weak-topology lower semicontinuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(F:\ell^2\to\mathbb R\) by \(F(x)=-\lVert x\rVert_2\). The functional is norm-continuous, while \(e_n\rightharpoonup0\) in \(\ell^2\) and \[F(0)=0> -1=\liminf_{n\to\infty}F(e_n).\] Thus lower semicontinuity in a stronger topology cannot be transferred automatically to a weaker topology; the chosen convergence topology must be compatible with the functional.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A norm-continuous functional may fail to be weakly lower semicontinuous, so the direct method must use lower semicontinuity in the compactness topology.
knowledge_statements.title: Topology-Compatibility Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The explicit ell^2 example correctly separates norm continuity from weak lower semicontinuity, and failure_boundary fits the topology-compatibility leaf. A specific authoritative source locator is absent.

children.title: Convex Integral-Functional Lower Semicontinuity
children.top_down_role: Convexity-based lower-semicontinuity for variational integrals.

assumptions_latex: \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d\) is measurable with finite measure and \(1<p<\infty\).
\(f:\Omega\times\mathbb R^m\to[0,+\infty]\) is measurable in \(x\), lower semicontinuous and convex in \(z\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(u_n\rightharpoonup u\) in \(L^p(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)\), then \(I(u)\leq\liminf_n I(u_n)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard weak lower-semicontinuity theorem for nonnegative convex normal integrands
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonnegative convex normal-integrand version on reflexive Lebesgue spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)\), set \[I(u)=\int_\Omega f(x,u(x))\,dx,\] with the integral allowed to equal \(+\infty\). Then \(I\) is sequentially weakly lower semicontinuous on \(L^p(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)\): whenever \(u_n\rightharpoonup u\), \[I(u)\leq\liminf_{n\to\infty}I(u_n).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Integrating a nonnegative lower-semicontinuous convex integrand produces a weakly lower-semicontinuous functional on a reflexive Lebesgue space.
knowledge_statements.title: Convex Integral-Functional Lower Semicontinuity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem is a standard convex-integral lower-semicontinuity result, but no source certifies that the stated measurability and lower-semicontinuity assumptions are sufficient in precisely this formulation. The theorem content kind fits the leaf.

children.title: Quasiconvex Lower Semicontinuity
children.top_down_role: Weak lower-semicontinuity regimes based on quasiconvex integrands.

assumptions_latex: \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d\) is bounded and Lipschitz, \(1<p<\infty\), and \(m\geq1\).
\(f:\mathbb R^{m\times d}\to\mathbb R\) is continuous, quasiconvex, and \(|f(A)|\leq C(1+|A|^p)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The functional \(I(u)=\int_\Omega f(\nabla u)\,dx\) is sequentially weakly lower semicontinuous on \(W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)\).

notation.meaning: Morrey quasiconvexity: comparison with compactly supported gradient perturbations

children.title: Polyconvex Lower Semicontinuity
children.top_down_role: Weak lower-semicontinuity regimes based on polyconvex structure.

assumptions_latex: \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d\) is bounded and Lipschitz and \(1<p<\infty\).
\(f:\mathbb R^{m\times d}\to\mathbb R\) is continuous, polyconvex, and \(|f(A)|\leq C(1+|A|^p)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The functional \(I(u)=\int_\Omega f(\nabla u)\,dx\) is sequentially weakly lower semicontinuous on \(W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)\).

notation.meaning: vector containing all minors of a matrix
convex representative of the polyconvex density

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: polyconvexity implies quasiconvexity, followed by the standard p-growth lower-semicontinuity theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Autonomous first-order integrals; polyconvexity is used as a sufficient condition for quasiconvexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Polyconvexity means that there is a convex function \(g\) on the finite-dimensional space of minors such that \(f(A)=g(M(A))\) for every \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times d}\). Such an \(f\) is quasiconvex. Consequently, if \(u_n\rightharpoonup u\) in \(W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)\), then \[\int_\Omega f(\nabla u)\,dx\leq\liminf_{n\to\infty}\int_\Omega f(\nabla u_n)\,dx.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polyconvexity supplies a convex representation through matrix minors and hence a sufficient route to weak lower semicontinuity.
knowledge_statements.title: Polyconvex Lower Semicontinuity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The polyconvex-to-quasiconvex route is standard and the theorem content kind fits the leaf, but the exact representation and lower-semicontinuity hypotheses have no inspectable supporting citation.

children.title: Vectorial Integral Regimes
children.top_down_role: Dimension-sensitive settings for vector-valued variational integrals.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^{m\times d}\to\mathbb R\) is a Borel density for a first-order autonomous integral.
\(Q\subset\mathbb R^d\) is any cube.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The vectorial weak lower-semicontinuity condition is Morrey quasiconvexity; when \(m=1\) or \(d=1\), it reduces to ordinary convexity.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Morrey quasiconvexity is the local gradient-variation condition governing vectorial first-order integrals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes genuinely vectorial problems from scalar or one-dimensional regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The relevant vectorial condition is \[f(A)\leq\frac1{|Q|}\int_Q f(A+\nabla\varphi(y))\,dy\] for every \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times d}\) and every \(\varphi\in W^{1,\infty}_0(Q;\mathbb R^m)\). For scalar-valued maps \(m=1\), or for one-dimensional domains \(d=1\), this condition is equivalent to convexity of \(f\). When \(m,d\geq2\), it is generally strictly weaker than convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Vectorial gradient integrals are governed by quasiconvexity; only scalar-valued or one-dimensional regimes collapse this condition to ordinary convexity.
knowledge_statements.title: Vectorial Integral Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The quasiconvexity formula and its reduction to convexity when m=1 or d=1 fit the regime leaf. Calling quasiconvexity the weak lower-semicontinuity condition can require regularity and growth hypotheses not stated here, so a source is needed to fix the intended scope.

children.title: Convexity-Gap Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Separations among convexity notions relevant to lower semicontinuity.

assumptions_latex: Matrices belong to \(\mathbb R^{3\times2}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Rank-one convexity is strictly weaker than quasiconvexity and therefore cannot alone guarantee weak lower semicontinuity of vectorial integral functionals.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical multidimensional counterexamples separate rank-one convexity from quasiconvexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical multidimensional separation; the exact counterexample and hypotheses require source certification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: There exists a finite-valued function \(f:\mathbb R^{3\times2}\to\mathbb R\) whose restriction \(t\mapsto f(A+t(a\otimes b))\) is convex for every \(A\), \(a\), and \(b\), but for which some cube \(Q\), matrix \(A\), and \(\varphi\in W^{1,\infty}_0(Q;\mathbb R^3)\) satisfy \[f(A)>\frac1{|Q|}\int_Q f(A+\nabla\varphi(y))\,dy.\] Thus rank-one convexity does not imply quasiconvexity in general.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In genuinely vectorial dimensions, rank-one convexity need not imply quasiconvexity, so it is insufficient by itself for weak lower semicontinuity.
knowledge_statements.title: Convexity-Gap Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The claimed 3-by-2 separation of rank-one convexity from quasiconvexity is a specialized counterexample and cannot be certified by standard-field rationale alone. The failure_boundary content kind is appropriate, but an exact source and locator are required.

children.title: Equi-Coercive Approximation
children.top_down_role: Uniform compactness control across approximating problems.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a topological space and \(F_n:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((F_n)\) is equi-coercive exactly when every common level union \(\bigcup_n\{F_n\leq c\}\) is contained in one compact set.

notation.meaning: sublevel set of the nth functional

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Topological definition used with Gamma-convergence and minimizer compactness.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 4. Set Convergence p. 108
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The sequence \((F_n)\) is equi-coercive if, for every \(c\in\mathbb R\), there exists a compact set \(K_c\subset X\) such that \[\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}\{x\in X:F_n(x)\leq c\}\subset K_c.\] In a metric space, the sequential variant requires every sequence \((x_n)\) with \(\sup_nF_n(x_n)<+\infty\) to possess a convergent subsequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equi-coercivity places every uniformly bounded family of sublevel points from all approximating functionals inside a common compact set.
knowledge_statements.title: Equi-Coercive Approximation

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 4. Set Convergence p. 108
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cited page is not a specific equi-coercivity definition locator. Moreover, the stated metric-space sequential variant only tests matched-index sequences x_n and is not equivalent to compact containment of the union of all indexed sublevels without a stronger formulation covering arbitrary index subsequences or all pairs (n,x). Source support is needed before choosing the exact definition.

\((F_n)\) is equi-coercive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lim_{n\to\infty}\inf_XF_n=\min_XF\).

notation.meaning: minimum value of the nth problem
minimum value of the limit problem

children.title: Convergence of Minimizer Sequences
children.top_down_role: Cluster behavior of exact or approximate minimizers.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is metric, \(F_n\) Gamma-converges to a proper \(F\), and \((F_n)\) is equi-coercive.
\(F_n(x_n)\leq\inf_XF_n+\varepsilon_n\) with \(\varepsilon_n\to0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every cluster point of \((x_n)\) lies in \(\operatorname*{argmin}_XF\); uniqueness of the minimizer implies \(x_n\to\bar x\).

notation.meaning: set of global minimizers of the limit functional

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compactness and identification of approximate minimizer limits under Gamma-convergence.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 4. Set Convergence p. 108
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The sequence \((x_n)\) is relatively compact. If a subsequence satisfies \(x_{n_k}\to\bar x\), then \[F(\bar x)=\min_{x\in X}F(x),\qquad F_{n_k}(x_{n_k})\to\min_{x\in X}F(x).\] Hence every cluster point is a minimizer of \(F\). If \(\operatorname*{argmin}_XF=\{\bar x\}\), relative compactness and uniqueness yield convergence of the full sequence \(x_n\to\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every cluster point of equi-coercive approximate minimizers minimizes the Gamma-limit; a unique limit minimizer forces convergence of the whole sequence.
knowledge_statements.title: Convergence of Minimizer Sequences

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 4. Set Convergence p. 108
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cluster-point and uniqueness conclusions are standard consequences of equi-coercive Gamma-convergence for approximate minimizers, and theorem is the correct content kind. The cited generic set-convergence page does not specifically support this result.

children.title: Solution-Set Stability
children.top_down_role: Set-level persistence of minimizing solutions under approximation.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is metric, \(F_n\) Gamma-converges to a proper \(F\), and \((F_n)\) is equi-coercive.
\(S_n=\operatorname*{argmin}_XF_n\) and \(S=\operatorname*{argmin}_XF\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{Limsup}_{n\to\infty}S_n\subset S\), while the reverse inclusion is not guaranteed by Gamma-convergence alone.

notation.meaning: minimizer sets of the approximating and limit problems

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Outer stability of exact solution sets; inner stability needs additional recovery of individual minimizers.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 4. Set Convergence p. 108
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(n_k\to\infty\), \(x_k\in S_{n_k}\), and \(x_k\to x\), then \(x\in S\). Equivalently, \[\operatorname*{Limsup}_{n\to\infty}S_n\subset S.\] Gamma-convergence and equi-coercivity alone do not imply \(S\subset\operatorname*{Liminf}_{n\to\infty}S_n\); that stronger inclusion requires approximating minimizers converging to each prescribed point of \(S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Limits of approximating minimizers remain solutions of the limit problem, but not every limit solution must be approximated by exact minimizers.
knowledge_statements.title: Solution-Set Stability

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 4. Set Convergence p. 108
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The outer-limit inclusion is the appropriate solution-set stability property, and the warning about failure of inner stability is appropriate. However, the assumptions do not ensure that each exact minimizer set S_n is nonempty, and the generic source locator does not certify the stated set-convergence result or its intended treatment of empty sets.

children.title: Attainment-Loss Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Approximation regimes where limiting values or solutions lose attainment.

assumptions_latex: For \(n\geq1\), define \(F_n:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) by \(F_n(x)=e^x+x^2/n\).
\(F:\mathbb R\to(0,+\infty)\) is given by \(F(x)=e^x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Although each \(F_n\) attains its minimum and \(F_n\) Gamma-converges to \(F\), the limit infimum \(0\) is not attained because equi-coercivity fails.

notation.meaning: unique minimizer of the nth functional

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: explicit locally uniform convergence and escaping-minimizer construction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit loss of attainment caused by minimizers escaping to infinity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Each \(F_n\) is continuous and coercive, hence has a unique minimizer \(x_n<0\) determined by \(e^{x_n}+2x_n/n=0\). The convergence \(F_n\to F\) is locally uniform and therefore implies Gamma-convergence on \(\mathbb R\). Nevertheless, \(x_n\to-\infty\), \[\min_{x\in\mathbb R}F_n(x)\to0=\inf_{x\in\mathbb R}F(x),\] and \(F(x)>0\) for every finite \(x\). Thus \(F\) does not attain its infimum, and \((F_n)\) is not equi-coercive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Coercive approximating problems can have minimizers escaping to infinity, leaving a Gamma-limit whose infimum is finite but unattained.
knowledge_statements.title: Attainment-Loss Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The explicit example is mathematically coherent: the minimizers escape to minus infinity, local uniform convergence gives Gamma-convergence, and the limit fails to attain its infimum. Counterexample is the correct content kind, but no inspectable authoritative source locator is supplied.
