children.title: Nonattainment Mechanisms
children.top_down_role: Geometric and topological sources of nonattainment.

children.title: Escape to Infinity
children.top_down_role: Loss of compactness through unbounded minimizing sequences.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a metric space and \(F:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is bounded below.
\((x_n)\subset X\) is a minimizing sequence: \(F(x_n)\to\inf_X F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((x_n)\) has no convergent subsequence, so compactness-based attainment fails.

notation.meaning: Sublevel set of the objective at height alpha.
Distance from the fixed reference point.

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Metric-space form of nonattainment caused by failure of boundedness or coercivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(x_0\in X\). Escape to infinity occurs when a minimizing sequence \((x_n)\) satisfies \(d(x_n,x_0)\to\infty\); more generally, it occurs when \((x_n)\) eventually leaves every compact subset of \(X\). Consequently, \((x_n)\) has no convergent subsequence and the direct compactness argument cannot produce a minimizer. In a proper metric space, the condition \(d(x_n,x_0)\to\infty\) is equivalent to eventual escape from every compact set. A sufficient boundary mechanism is failure of inf-compactness: some sublevel set \(S_\alpha\) containing a minimizing tail is noncompact and admits such an escaping sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A minimizing sequence escapes to infinity when it leaves every compact set, preventing extraction of a convergent subsequence and hence compactness-based attainment.
knowledge_statements.title: Escape to Infinity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits the leaf, but no citation supports the proper-space equivalence or the stated inf-compactness mechanism.

children.title: Loss of Feasible Closure
children.top_down_role: Failure of limit feasibility.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a topological space, \(C\subset X\), and \(F:C\to(-\infty,+\infty]\).
\((x_n)\subset C\) is minimizing and converges to \(x\in X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(x\notin C\), the limiting candidate is infeasible and attainment in \(C\) does not follow.

notation.meaning: Closure of the feasible set in the chosen topology.
Infimum of the objective over the feasible set.

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of the closed-feasible-set step in the direct method.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Loss of feasible closure is the mechanism in which \(x_n\in C\), \(F(x_n)\to m\), and \(x_n\to x\in\overline C\), but \(x\notin C\). Thus the topology supplies a limit, yet feasibility is not preserved. Even if an extension \(\widetilde F:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is lower semicontinuous and satisfies \(\widetilde F(x)\leq\liminf_n F(x_n)=m\), the point \(x\) cannot attain the original problem over \(C\). Replacing \(C\) by \(\overline C\) defines a relaxation and may lower the optimal value unless every newly feasible limit has value at least \(m\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convergent minimizing sequence may approach a point outside a nonclosed feasible set, so its limit cannot solve the original constrained problem.
knowledge_statements.title: Loss of Feasible Closure

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure mechanism fits the leaf, but the extension argument requires an explicit condition relating the extension to F on C, and no source is supplied.

children.title: Loss of Lower Semicontinuity
children.top_down_role: Failure of objective-value passage to limits.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a topological space and \(F:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\).
\((x_n)\) is minimizing and \(x_n\to x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(F(x)>\liminf_nF(x_n)\), the limit need not attain \(\inf_XF\).

notation.meaning: Sequential lower limit along the minimizing sequence.

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential form of objective-value failure in the direct method.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Loss of lower semicontinuity along a minimizing sequence occurs when \(x_n\to x\), \(F(x_n)\to m\), but \(F(x)>\liminf_{n\to\infty}F(x_n)=m\). Although compactness yields the candidate \(x\), objective values do not pass to the limit in the direction required for minimality. Hence \(x\) need not minimize \(F\), and the direct method fails at the lower-semicontinuity step. Equivalently, sequential lower semicontinuity fails at \(x\) whenever some convergent sequence satisfies \(F(x)>\liminf_nF(x_n)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the objective jumps upward at the limit of a minimizing sequence, the limiting point need not be a minimizer despite compactness.
knowledge_statements.title: Loss of Lower Semicontinuity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The sequential lower-semicontinuity failure is mathematically standard and the content kind fits, but the record has no inspectable citation.

children.title: Oscillation-Concentration Defect Family
children.top_down_role: Fine-scale behavior beyond ordinary function limits.

children.title: Fine-Scale Oscillation
children.top_down_role: Rapidly varying minimizing behavior beyond ordinary function limits.

assumptions_latex: \(Q=(0,1)^d\), \(1\leq p<\infty\), and \(a:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) is bounded, nonconstant, periodic, and has zero cell average.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(u_n\rightharpoonup0\) in \(L^p(Q)\), but \((u_n)\) has no strongly convergent subsequence.
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Periodic example exhibiting weak convergence without strong compactness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(u_n(x)=a(nx)\) for \(x\in Q\). Periodic averaging gives \(u_n\rightharpoonup0\) in \(L^p(Q)\), while \(\|u_n\|_{L^p(Q)}\to\|a\|_{L^p(Y)}>0\). Moreover, \(\|u_n-u_m\|_{L^p(Q)}\) does not generally tend to zero as \(m,n\to\infty\). Thus no subsequence converges strongly to the weak limit. The nonzero microscopic amplitudes persist at scales tending to zero, so ordinary pointwise or strong limits discard information that can instead be represented by a nontrivial Young measure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Periodic oscillations at vanishing scales converge weakly to their average while retaining nonzero norm, thereby destroying strong compactness.
knowledge_statements.title: Fine-Scale Oscillation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample kind fits, but periodic weak convergence and the Young-measure interpretation require an authoritative source.

children.title: Mass Concentration
children.top_down_role: Localization of mass or energy on progressively smaller regions.

assumptions_latex: \(1\leq p<\infty\), \(x_0\in\mathbb R^d\), and \(0\neq\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(u_n\to0\) almost everywhere while \(|u_n|^p\,dx\stackrel{*}{\rightharpoonup}\|\varphi\|_p^p\delta_{x_0}\).

notation.meaning: Dirac measure at the concentration point.

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scaling example of norm concentration at one point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Set \(u_n(x)=n^{d/p}\varphi(n(x-x_0))\). A change of variables yields \(\|u_n\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^d)}=\|\varphi\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^d)}\) for every \(n\), while \(u_n(x)\to0\) for almost every \(x\neq x_0\). For every \(\psi\in C_c(\mathbb R^d)\), one has \(\int\psi(x)|u_n(x)|^p\,dx\to\psi(x_0)\|\varphi\|_p^p\). Hence the energy densities converge weak-star as measures to \(\|\varphi\|_p^p\delta_{x_0}\), although the ordinary almost-everywhere limit carries none of that mass.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rescaled bump shrinks to one point while preserving its norm, producing a Dirac mass invisible in its almost-everywhere limit.
knowledge_statements.title: Mass Concentration

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The concentrating-bump counterexample is precise and fits the leaf, but no citation supports the measure-convergence claim.

children.title: Mixed Oscillation–Concentration Regimes
children.top_down_role: Coupled fine-scale effects requiring generalized limit objects.

assumptions_latex: \(1\leq p<\infty\), \(a\) is bounded, periodic, nonconstant, and \(\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d)\setminus\{0\}\).
\(x_0\in\mathbb R^d\) and \(a\varphi\not\equiv0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The sequence simultaneously develops microscopic value oscillations and a spatially concentrated \(p\)-energy measure.

notation.meaning: Cell average over the periodicity cell.

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete sequence coupling two separated microscopic scales.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(u_n(x)=n^{d/p}a(n^2(x-x_0))\varphi(n(x-x_0))\). Its support contracts toward \(x_0\), while the factor \(a(n^2(x-x_0))\) oscillates on a finer scale inside that support. Periodic averaging and rescaling give \(|u_n|^p\,dx\stackrel{*}{\rightharpoonup}\langle|a|^p\rangle_Y\|\varphi\|_p^p\delta_{x_0}\). At the same time, the values sampled near \(x_0\) retain the distribution of \(a\), rather than a single amplitude. Thus neither an ordinary weak limit nor a concentration measure alone records the complete limiting behavior.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A concentrating bump carrying faster periodic oscillations exhibits both a Dirac energy defect and unresolved microscopic value distributions.
knowledge_statements.title: Mixed Oscillation–Concentration Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample role fits, but measurability of a is unstated and the coupled oscillation-concentration interpretation needs authoritative support.

children.title: Ordinary-Limit Failure
children.top_down_role: Boundaries of representation by conventional function-space limits.

assumptions_latex: \((u_n)\) is bounded in \(L^p(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)\) for some \(1<p<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Weak convergence alone need not determine limits of nonlinear quantities \(g(u_n)\).

notation.meaning: Weak limit in the reflexive Lebesgue space.

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary of ordinary weak-limit descriptions for nonlinear variational energies.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Even when a subsequence satisfies \(u_nightharpoonup u\) in \(L^p(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)\), it need not follow that \(g(u_n)\rightharpoonup g(u)\) in \(L^1(\Omega)\) for continuous nonlinear \(g\) of \(p\)-growth. Fine-scale oscillation can make the weak limit of \(g(u_n)\) depend on a distribution of values, while concentration can create a singular measure not represented by \(u\). Therefore the ordinary weak limit is generally insufficient for passing nonlinear objectives to the limit; Young measures or generalized Young measures may be required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weak limits can lose oscillatory distributions and concentrated mass, so they may not determine limits of nonlinear energy densities.
knowledge_statements.title: Ordinary-Limit Failure

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits, but the claims about nonlinear weak limits, concentration, and generalized Young measures lack a source and require carefully stated growth conditions.

children.title: Relaxation Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Chapter-local navigation to standard closures and generalized minimizers.

children.title: Lower-Semicontinuous Envelopes
children.top_down_role: Topological closure of objective models.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a topological space and \(F:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\overline F\) is the greatest lower-semicontinuous function satisfying \(\overline F\leq F\).
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Topological lower-semicontinuous minorant envelope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The lower-semicontinuous envelope of \(F\) is defined by
\[\overline F(x)=\sup_{U\in\mathcal N(x)}\inf_{y\in U}F(y).\]
It satisfies \(\overline F\leq F\), is lower semicontinuous, and dominates every lower-semicontinuous function \(G:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) with \(G\leq F\). If \(X\) is first countable, then
\[\overline F(x)=\inf\left\{\liminf_{n\to\infty}F(x_n):x_n\to x\right\}.\]
Thus minimizing the envelope is the canonical relaxation associated with the chosen topology; changing that topology can change the envelope.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The lower-semicontinuous envelope is the greatest lower-semicontinuous minorant of an objective and admits a neighborhood, or sequential, relaxation formula.
knowledge_statements.title: Lower-Semicontinuous Envelopes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind fits, but the neighborhood and first-countable sequential formulas need a citation; the envelope may take minus infinity unless additional boundedness is imposed or its codomain is enlarged.

children.title: Convexity-Adapted Envelope Family
children.top_down_role: Geometry-adapted relaxation of nonconvex models.

children.title: Convex Envelopes
children.top_down_role: Convex relaxation for scalar or finite-dimensional nonconvex models.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^m\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and bounded below by an affine function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f^{**}\) is the greatest lower-semicontinuous convex minorant of \(f\).
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional lower-semicontinuous convex envelope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The lower-semicontinuous convex envelope of \(f\) is its Fenchel biconjugate
\[f^{**}(x)=\sup_{z\in\mathbb R^m}\{\langle z,x\rangle-f^*(z)\}.\]
It is convex and lower semicontinuous, satisfies \(f^{**}\leq f\), and dominates every lower-semicontinuous convex function \(g\) with \(g\leq f\). Equivalently,
\[f^{**}(x)=\inf\left\{\liminf_{n\to\infty}\sum_{i=1}^{k_n}\lambda_{n,i}f(x_{n,i}):\sum_i\lambda_{n,i}x_{n,i}\to x,\ \lambda_{n,i}\geq0,\ \sum_i\lambda_{n,i}=1\right\}.\]
If \(f\) is already lower semicontinuous and convex, then \(f^{**}=f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Fenchel biconjugate is the greatest lower-semicontinuous convex function below the original integrand.
knowledge_statements.title: Convex Envelopes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind fits, but both the Fenchel–Moreau characterization and the stated sequential barycentric formula require an inspectable source.

children.title: Quasiconvex Envelopes
children.top_down_role: Relaxation adapted to vectorial gradient structures.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^{m\times d}\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is Borel measurable and bounded below.
\(Y=(0,1)^d\), and perturbations belong to \(W_0^{1,\infty}(Y;\mathbb R^m)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Qf\) is the greatest quasiconvex minorant of \(f\) under the stated cell-formula hypotheses.
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Morrey quasiconvex envelope for first-order gradient integrands.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A function \(g:\mathbb R^{m\times d}\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is quasiconvex when, for every \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times d}\) and \(\phi\in W_0^{1,\infty}(Y;\mathbb R^m)\),
\[g(A)\leq\int_Y g(A+\nabla\phi(y))\,dy.\]
The quasiconvex envelope is
\[Qf(A)=\sup\{g(A):g\leq f,\ g\text{ is quasiconvex}\}.\]
Under standard continuity and growth assumptions ensuring the cell representation, it is equivalently given by the appropriate relaxed cell formula obtained by infimizing \(\int_Y f(A+\nabla\phi)\,dy\) over zero-boundary microscopic perturbations, with multicell relaxation when required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The quasiconvex envelope is the greatest quasiconvex minorant and, under suitable growth and continuity assumptions, has a microscopic cell representation.
knowledge_statements.title: Quasiconvex Envelopes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind fits, but the assumptions do not specify the continuity and growth hypotheses under which the one-cell or multicell formula is valid.

children.title: Envelope Selection Regimes
children.top_down_role: Model features determining the appropriate geometric envelope.

assumptions_latex: The relaxation topology and admissible microscopic perturbations are fixed before taking the envelope.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The correct envelope is selected by the convergence mode and differential constraints, not by the integrand alone.

notation.meaning: Convex envelope of a zero-order integrand.
Quasiconvex envelope of a gradient integrand.

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Selection rule for common relaxation envelopes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an objective \(F\), relaxation first selects the greatest minorant that is lower semicontinuous in the prescribed topology \(\tau\), namely \(\operatorname{cl}_{\tau}F\). For zero-order integral functionals under weak convergence, unrestricted mixing of values typically selects the lower-semicontinuous convex envelope \(f^{**}\). For first-order functionals \(F(u)=\int_\Omega f(\nabla u(x))\,dx\) under weak Sobolev convergence, gradient compatibility restricts microscopic mixtures and typically selects the lower-semicontinuous quasiconvex envelope \(Qf\). Additional differential constraints may require corresponding constrained convexity notions. Therefore envelope choice is determined jointly by topology, locality, and admissible perturbations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weak zero-order mixing generally selects convexification, whereas weak gradient relaxation selects quasiconvexification; topology and differential constraints govern the choice.
knowledge_statements.title: Envelope Selection Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle kind fits, but the convexification and quasiconvexification regimes are stated too generally without functional, topology, growth, and admissibility hypotheses or supporting citations.

children.title: Envelope-Gap Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Differences between original energies and their relaxed envelopes.

assumptions_latex: \(E f\) is the envelope selected by the topology and admissible perturbations, with \(Ef\leq f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The pointwise envelope gap is nonzero exactly where \(Ef<f\); an optimization-value gap additionally requires access to that region.
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes pointwise envelope gaps from gaps in optimal values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(\Delta_f(x)=f(x)-Ef(x)\in[0,+\infty]\). The envelope is exact at \(x\) precisely when \(\Delta_f(x)=0\), and a pointwise relaxation gap occurs precisely when \(Ef(x)<f(x)\). For a variational problem with original infimum \(m\) and relaxed infimum \(\overline m\), one always has \(\overline m\leq m\). A strict value gap \(\overline m<m\) can occur only when admissible relaxed competitors exploit states or microstructures where the selected envelope is strictly below the original density. Conversely, a pointwise gap need not change the infimum if every minimizing competitor avoids the gap region.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An envelope differs from the original function exactly on its pointwise gap set, but the optimal value changes only when admissible competitors exploit that set.
knowledge_statements.title: Envelope-Gap Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits, but f-Ef is undefined where both values are positive infinity, and the asserted necessary mechanism for a strict value gap needs a precise formulation and source.

children.title: Generalized Minimizer Representation Family
children.top_down_role: Generalized limit objects for oscillation and concentration.

children.title: Measure-Valued Generalized Minimizers
children.top_down_role: Generalized minimizing objects represented through measures.

assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal A\) is a nonempty admissible set in a Hausdorff state space \(Z\).
\(F:Z\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is Borel measurable and bounded below on \(\mathcal A\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\displaystyle \int_Z F(z)\,d\mu^*(z)=\inf_{\mu\in\mathcal P(\mathcal A)}\int_Z F(z)\,d\mu(z)\).

notation.meaning: Borel probability measures supported on the admissible set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Probability-measure relaxation on an admissible state space; the intended relation to Young measures requires source confirmation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A measure-valued generalized minimizer of \(F\) over \(\mathcal A\) is a probability measure \(\mu^*\in\mathcal P(\mathcal A)\) for which \(F\) is \(\mu^*\)-integrable and
\[
\int_Z F(z)\,d\mu^*(z)=\inf_{\mu\in\mathcal P(\mathcal A)}\int_Z F(z)\,d\mu(z).
\]
If additional constraints are expressed through moments or barycenters, \(\mathcal P(\mathcal A)\) is replaced by the corresponding weakly closed subset of probability measures satisfying those constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A measure-valued minimizer is an admissible probability distribution attaining the least expected energy, with any prescribed moment or barycenter constraints imposed on the distribution.
knowledge_statements.title: Measure-Valued Generalized Minimizers

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source supports this probability-measure relaxation or its intended relation to Young measures. The unconstrained formulation also reduces to randomization over ordinary admissible states, so its status as a generalized-minimizer representation depends on the intended convention.

children.title: Parametrized Generalized Minimizers
children.top_down_role: Spatially indexed generalized limits for fine-scale behavior.

assumptions_latex: \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d\) is measurable with finite measure.
\(f:\Omega\times\mathbb R^m\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is a normal integrand bounded below by an integrable function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
\(\displaystyle \mathcal I(
u^*)=\inf_{
u\in\mathcal Y}\int_\Omega\int_{\mathbb R^m}f(x,\xi)\,d
u_x(\xi)\,dx\).

notation.meaning: admissible class of weakly measurable probability kernels
probability measure assigned to the parameter point x

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Young-measure interpretation with the physical variable as parameter; admissibility may include barycentric or differential constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A parametrized generalized minimizer is a weakly measurable family \(\nu^*=\{\nu_x^*\}_{x\in\Omega}\) of Borel probability measures on \(\mathbb R^m\), belonging to a specified admissible class \(\mathcal Y\), such that
\[
\mathcal I(\nu^*):=\int_\Omega\int_{\mathbb R^m}f(x,\xi)\,d\nu_x^*(\xi)\,dx
=
\inf_{\nu\in\mathcal Y}\int_\Omega\int_{\mathbb R^m}f(x,\xi)\,d\nu_x(\xi)\,dx.
\]
Any pointwise, barycentric, or differential constraint defining the relaxation is included in \(\mathcal Y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A parametrized generalized minimizer is a measurable probability kernel that satisfies the relaxed constraints and minimizes the energy obtained by averaging the integrand at each parameter point.
knowledge_statements.title: Parametrized Generalized Minimizers

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Young-measure formulation is plausible and the representation content kind fits, but the admissible kernel class and any barycentric or differential constraints are essential to the mathematical meaning and require an authoritative source.

children.title: Oscillation Representation
children.top_down_role: Generalized limit objects capturing unresolved oscillatory structure.

assumptions_latex: \(1\le p<\infty\) and \((u_j)\) is bounded in \(L^p(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)\).
\(g:\Omega\times\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R\) is Carathéodory and \((g(\cdot,u_j))\) is uniformly integrable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\displaystyle g(\cdot,u_j)\rightharpoonup \bigl[x\mapsto\int g(x,\xi)\,d\nu_x(\xi)\bigr]\) weakly in \(L^1(\Omega)\) along a subsequence.

notation.meaning: Young measure generated by a subsequence

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical Young-measure representation of oscillation for an equiintegrable composition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
There exist a subsequence, not relabeled, and a weakly measurable family \((\nu_x)_{x\in\Omega}\) of Borel probability measures on \(\mathbb R^m\) such that, for every Carathéodory integrand \(g\) whose compositions \((g(\cdot,u_j))\) are uniformly integrable,
\[
g(\cdot,u_j)\rightharpoonup \left[x\mapsto\int_{\mathbb R^m}g(x,\xi)\,d\nu_x(\xi)\right]
\quad\text{weakly in }L^1(\Omega).
\]
Thus \(\nu_x\) records the limiting distribution of bounded-scale oscillations at almost every \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded sequence has a subsequence whose nonlinear, uniformly integrable observations converge to averages against a pointwise probability measure describing its oscillations.
knowledge_statements.title: Oscillation Representation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is a standard Young-measure oscillation representation and the content kind fits, but no citation is supplied for the subsequence theorem, measurability conditions, or uniformly integrable composition conclusion.

children.title: Concentration Representation
children.top_down_role: Generalized limit objects retaining concentrated mass or energy.

assumptions_latex: \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d\) is bounded and \((u_j)\) is bounded in \(L^1(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)\).
\(f\) is continuous with linear growth and has a continuous recession function \(f^\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\displaystyle f(u_j)\,dx\stackrel{*}{\rightharpoonup}\langle f,\nu_x\rangle\,dx+\langle f^\infty,\nu_x^\infty\rangle\,d\lambda\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generalized Young-measure representation for linear-growth integrands and concentration at infinity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
After passage to a subsequence, there are a Young measure \((\nu_x)\), a finite positive measure \(\lambda\) on \(\overline\Omega\), and a \(\lambda\)-measurable family \((\nu_x^\infty)\) of probability measures on the unit sphere such that
\[
f(u_j)\,dx\stackrel{*}{\rightharpoonup}
\left(\int_{\mathbb R^m}f(\xi)\,d\nu_x(\xi)\right)dx+
\left(\int_{\mathbb S^{m-1}}f^\infty(\theta)\,d\nu_x^\infty(\theta)\right)d\lambda
\]
as finite Radon measures. The second term represents concentration magnitude and direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A generalized Young measure separates nonlinear limits into an oscillation average and a singular term encoding the magnitude and directions of concentration.
knowledge_statements.title: Concentration Representation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The oscillation–concentration decomposition is plausible, but the precise generalized Young-measure convention, domain of the concentration measure, recession-function hypotheses, and measure convergence require source confirmation.

children.title: Complete-Metric-Space Forms
children.top_down_role: Canonical metric-space formulations.

assumptions_latex: \((X,d)\) is complete and \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and bounded below.
\(\varepsilon>0\), \(\lambda>0\), and \(f(x_0)\le\inf_X f+\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d(x_\varepsilon,x_0)\le\lambda\) and \(f(x)>f(x_\varepsilon)-(\varepsilon/\lambda)d(x,x_\varepsilon)\) for every \(x\ne x_\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard two-parameter complete-metric-space form of Ekeland's variational principle.

source_refs.locator: 2.3 Relations with Variational Principles p. 203
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
There exists \(x_\varepsilon\in X\) such that
\[
f(x_\varepsilon)\le f(x_0),\qquad d(x_\varepsilon,x_0)\le\lambda,
\]
and
\[
f(x)>f(x_\varepsilon)-\frac{\varepsilon}{\lambda}d(x,x_\varepsilon)
\quad\text{for every }x\in X\setminus\{x_\varepsilon\}.
\]
Equivalently, \(x_\varepsilon\) is the unique strict minimizer of \(x\mapsto f(x)+(\varepsilon/\lambda)d(x,x_\varepsilon)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every approximate minimizer of a lower semicontinuous bounded-below function on a complete metric space lies near a point that strictly minimizes a linearly perturbed objective.
knowledge_statements.title: Complete-Metric-Space Forms

children.title: Localized Forms
children.top_down_role: Neighborhood-restricted perturbational principles.

assumptions_latex: \((X,d)\) is complete and \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and bounded below.
\(f(x_0)\le\inf_X f+\varepsilon\) and \(\rho>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_\varepsilon\in\overline B(x_0,\rho)\) and \(f(x)>f(x_\varepsilon)-(\varepsilon/\rho)d(x,x_\varepsilon)\) for all \(x\ne x_\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ekeland's principle with a prescribed radius and corresponding perturbation slope.

source_refs.locator: 2.3 Relations with Variational Principles p. 203
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
There exists \(x_\varepsilon\in X\) satisfying
\[
d(x_\varepsilon,x_0)\le\rho,
\qquad f(x_\varepsilon)\le f(x_0),
\]
and
\[
f(x)>f(x_\varepsilon)-\frac{\varepsilon}{\rho}d(x,x_\varepsilon)
\quad\text{for every }x\in X\setminus\{x_\varepsilon\}.
\]
Hence the improved point is localized in \(\overline B(x_0,\rho)\), while the strength of the perturbation is exactly controlled by the ratio \(\varepsilon/\rho\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choosing a radius localizes the improved point within that radius, at the cost of a perturbation slope equal to the approximation error divided by the radius.
knowledge_statements.title: Localized Forms

knowledge_statements.title: Constrained Forms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed-feasible-set form of Ekeland's variational principle on the complete restricted metric space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
There exists \(x_\varepsilon\in C\) such that
\[
f(x_\varepsilon)\le f(x_0),\qquad d(x_\varepsilon,x_0)\le\lambda,
\]
and
\[
f(x)>f(x_\varepsilon)-\frac{\varepsilon}{\lambda}d(x,x_\varepsilon)
\quad\text{for every }x\in C\setminus\{x_\varepsilon\}.
\]
Both the selected point and all comparison points are feasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a nonempty closed feasible subset of a complete metric space, Ekeland's point remains feasible and satisfies the strict perturbed minimality inequality against every other feasible point.
assumptions_latex: \((X,d)\) is complete, \(C\subset X\) is nonempty and closed, and \(f:C\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and bounded below.
\(x_0\in C\), \(\varepsilon>0\), \(\lambda>0\), and \(f(x_0)\le\inf_C f+\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_\varepsilon\in C\), \(d(x_\varepsilon,x_0)\le\lambda\), and \(f(x)>f(x_\varepsilon)-(\varepsilon/\lambda)d(x,x_\varepsilon)\) for every \(x\in C\setminus\{x_\varepsilon\}\).

children.title: Feasible-Neighborhood Forms

knowledge_statements.title: Feasible-Neighborhood Forms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ekeland's principle on a closed feasible neighborhood, with the selected point localized inside the neighborhood radius.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
There exists \(x_\varepsilon\in D\) such that
\[
f(x_\varepsilon)\le f(x_0),\qquad d(x_\varepsilon,x_0)\le\lambda<r,
\]
and
\[
f(x)>f(x_\varepsilon)-\frac{\varepsilon}{\lambda}d(x,x_\varepsilon)
\quad\text{for every }x\in D\setminus\{x_\varepsilon\}.
\]
In particular, \(x_\varepsilon\in C\cap\overline B(x_0,\lambda)\), while the comparison inequality is asserted only on \(D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a closed feasible neighborhood, Ekeland's principle gives a feasible point within the chosen localization radius, with perturbed minimality asserted against points in that neighborhood.
assumptions_latex: \((X,d)\) is complete, \(C\subset X\) is closed, \(x_0\in C\), \(r>0\), and \(D=C\cap\overline B(x_0,r)\).
\(f:D\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and bounded below.
\(\varepsilon>0\), \(0<\lambda<r\), and \(f(x_0)\le\inf_D f+\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_\varepsilon\in C\cap\overline B(x_0,\lambda)\) and \(f(x)>f(x_\varepsilon)-(\varepsilon/\lambda)d(x,x_\varepsilon)\) for every \(x\in D\setminus\{x_\varepsilon\}\).

children.title: Boundary-Sensitive Regimes
children.top_down_role: Effects of feasible-set boundaries on localized perturbations.

assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a closed subset of a complete metric space and \(f:C\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) satisfies the constrained Ekeland hypotheses.
\(x_\varepsilon\in C\) is the resulting Ekeland point with perturbation slope \(\alpha>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|\nabla_C f|(x_\varepsilon)\le\alpha\), while no bound for \(|\nabla f|(x_\varepsilon)\) follows unless ambient competitors are locally feasible.

notation.meaning: strong slope computed using competitors in C
ambient strong slope when f has an ambient extension

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary points yield a relative slope estimate; an ambient slope estimate requires local interior feasibility.

source_refs.locator: 2.3.2 Subdifferential Variational Principles p. 206
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The constrained Ekeland inequality
\[
f(x)\ge f(x_\varepsilon)-\alpha d(x,x_\varepsilon)
\quad\text{for all }x\in C
\]
implies the relative strong-slope estimate \(|\nabla_C f|(x_\varepsilon)\le\alpha\). If \(x_\varepsilon\) is a boundary point of \(C\), this does not imply the corresponding ambient estimate \(|\nabla f|(x_\varepsilon)\le\alpha\), because descent directions leaving \(C\) are absent from the comparison. The ambient estimate follows when a neighborhood of \(x_\varepsilon\) is contained in \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a feasible boundary, Ekeland controls only the slope relative to feasible competitors; ambient descent can remain uncontrolled unless the selected point is locally interior.
knowledge_statements.title: Boundary-Sensitive Regimes

knowledge_statements.title: Extended-Real Forms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-real form of Ekeland's variational principle, including indicator-function representations of constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
There exists \(x_\varepsilon\in\operatorname{dom}f\) such that
\[
f(x_\varepsilon)\le f(x_0),\qquad d(x_\varepsilon,x_0)\le\lambda,
\]
and
\[
f(x)>f(x_\varepsilon)-\frac{\varepsilon}{\lambda}d(x,x_\varepsilon)
\quad\text{for every }x\in X\setminus\{x_\varepsilon\}.
\]
If \(C\subset X\) is closed and \(g+\delta_C\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and bounded below, applying this form to \(f=g+\delta_C\) yields the corresponding constrained formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Ekeland's principle applies to proper lower semicontinuous extended-real functions. A closed-set indicator encodes feasibility whenever the resulting function satisfies the theorem's hypotheses.
assumptions_latex: \((X,d)\) is complete and \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and bounded below.
\(x_0\in\operatorname{dom}f\), \(\varepsilon>0\), \(\lambda>0\), and \(f(x_0)\le\inf_X f+\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_\varepsilon\in\operatorname{dom}f\), \(d(x_\varepsilon,x_0)\le\lambda\), and \(f(x)>f(x_\varepsilon)-(\varepsilon/\lambda)d(x,x_\varepsilon)\) for every \(x\in X\setminus\{x_\varepsilon\}\).

notation.meaning: effective domain of the extended-real function
Ekeland point in the effective domain
indicator equal to zero on C and positive infinity outside C

children.title: Vector-Valued Forms
children.top_down_role: Perturbational principles for vector-valued objectives.

assumptions_latex: \((X,d)\) is complete, \(Y\) is a real topological vector space, and \(K\subset Y\) is a closed convex cone.
\(e\in\operatorname{int}K\), and the scalarization \(x\mapsto\varphi_e(F(x)-y_0)\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and bounded below.
\(\varphi_e(F(x_0)-y_0)\le\inf_X\varphi_e(F(\cdot)-y_0)+\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(x)-y_0\notin \varphi_e(F(x_*)-y_0)e-(\varepsilon/\lambda)d(x,x_*)e-\operatorname{int}K\) for every \(x\ne x_*\).

notation.meaning: cone scalarization defined by the displayed infimum

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A scalarization-derived vector form; stronger cone-order variants require a specified ordering convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(\lambda>0\), scalar Ekeland applied to \(x\mapsto\varphi_e(F(x)-y_0)\) yields \(x_*\in X\) with \(d(x_*,x_0)\le\lambda\), \(\varphi_e(F(x_*)-y_0)\le\varphi_e(F(x_0)-y_0)\), and
\[
\varphi_e(F(x)-y_0)>
\varphi_e(F(x_*)-y_0)-\frac{\varepsilon}{\lambda}d(x,x_*)
\]
for every \(x\ne x_*\). Equivalently, the vector \(F(x)-y_0\) cannot belong to \(\varphi_e(F(x_*)-y_0)e-(\varepsilon/\lambda)d(x,x_*)e-\operatorname{int}K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scalarizing a cone-ordered vector objective and applying Ekeland produces a nearby point satisfying a strict scalarized, and hence cone-exclusion, variational inequality.
knowledge_statements.title: Vector-Valued Forms

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The scalar Ekeland conclusion is plausible, but the claimed equivalence with the displayed cone-exclusion relation depends on exact properties of the Gerstewitz scalarization and the cone convention. An authoritative source is required before fixing the vector formulation.

children.title: Set-Valued Forms
children.top_down_role: Perturbational principles for multifunction or set-valued objectives.

assumptions_latex: \((X,d)\) is complete, \(Y\) is a real topological vector space, and \(K\subset Y\) is a closed convex cone with \(e\in\operatorname{int}K\).
\(G:X\rightrightarrows Y\) has nonempty values and \(m(x):=\inf_{y\in G(x)}\varphi_e(y-y_0)\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and bounded below.
\(m(x_0)\le\inf_Xm+\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(m(x)>m(x_*)-(\varepsilon/\lambda)d(x,x_*)\) for every \(x\ne x_*\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Infimal-scalarization form for a set-valued objective; direct set-order formulations depend on additional conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(\lambda>0\), Ekeland's principle applied to the scalar merit function \(m\) gives \(x_*\in X\) such that
\[
d(x_*,x_0)\le\lambda,
\u00a0\u00a0\u00a0\u00a0\u00a0\u00a0 m(x_*)\le m(x_0),
\]
and
\[
m(x)>m(x_*)-\frac{\varepsilon}{\lambda}d(x,x_*)
\quad\text{for every }x\in X\setminus\{x_*\}.
\]
Thus a set-valued optimization problem admits an Ekeland point whenever its infimal cone scalarization is an admissible extended-real objective. Any direct inclusion statement for \(G(x)+K\) additionally depends on the selected set order and attainment of the inner infimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set-valued problem inherits Ekeland's conclusion when its values define a proper lower semicontinuous infimal scalarization; direct set-order conclusions need additional conventions.
knowledge_statements.title: Set-Valued Forms

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Applying scalar Ekeland to the merit function is plausible, but no source supports this as the intended set-valued form. The relation to a genuine set order, inner-infimum attainment, and value closedness remains convention-dependent.

children.title: Order-Structured Extensions
children.top_down_role: Extensions governed by cones, partial orders, or preference relations.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a complete metric space and \(Y\) is a Hausdorff locally convex space ordered by a closed convex pointed cone \(K\).
\(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) has nonempty values, an appropriately closed graph, and is bounded below in the \(K\)-order.
\(k_0\in K\setminus\{0\}\), \(\varepsilon>0\), and \(\lambda>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bar x\) is minimal for the distance-perturbed order and lies within \(\lambda\) of the initial approximate minimizer.

notation.meaning: Ordering cone in the range space

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cone-ordered, set-valued Ekeland extension with a metric perturbation in a fixed positive direction.

source_refs.locator: 5.3.2 Generalized Order Optimality p. 73
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x_0\in X\) be an \(\varepsilon\)-approximate \(K\)-minimizer of \(F\). Under the stated order-completeness and closedness hypotheses, there exist \(\bar x\in X\) and \(\bar y\in F(\bar x)\) such that \(d(\bar x,x_0)\leq\lambda\), and for every \(x\neq\bar x\),
\[
F(x)\cap\left(\bar y-\frac{\varepsilon}{\lambda}d(x,\bar x)k_0-K\right)=\varnothing.
\]
Thus no distinct feasible image improves upon \(\bar y\) after charging the metric displacement in the ordered direction \(k_0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An approximate cone-minimizer can be localized to a nearby point that becomes minimal after adding a distance-dependent perturbation in a positive order direction.
knowledge_statements.title: Order-Structured Extensions

source_witnesses.locator: 5.3.2 Generalized Order Optimality p. 73

The cited section must be inspected for the exact order, completeness, and closedness hypotheses.

children.title: Scalarization Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Passage from ordered or set-valued problems to scalar variational forms.

assumptions_latex: \(Y\) is a Hausdorff locally convex space and \(K\subset Y\) is a closed convex cone.
\(K^+:=\{y^*\in Y^*: \langle y^*,k\rangle\geq0\text{ for all }k\in K\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Cone comparisons are exactly the simultaneous scalar comparisons generated by \(K^+\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual-cone scalarization of cone comparisons used by ordered vector and set-valued variational principles.

source_refs.locator: 5.3.2 Generalized Order Optimality p. 73
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(y_1,y_2\in Y\), separation of the closed convex cone gives
\[
y_1\leq_K y_2\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \langle y^*,y_1\rangle\leq\langle y^*,y_2\rangle\ \text{for every }y^*\in K^+.
\]
Consequently, an ordered perturbation \(y\mapsto y+\alpha k_0\), with \(k_0\in K\) and \(\alpha\geq0\), becomes the scalar penalty \(\alpha\langle y^*,k_0\rangle\) under each \(y^*\in K^+\). Any strict scalar minimum for one normalized \(y^*\), where \(\langle y^*,k_0\rangle=1\), excludes domination detectable by that scalarization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive dual functionals convert cone comparisons and ordered metric perturbations into scalar inequalities and scalar penalties.
knowledge_statements.title: Scalarization Interfaces

children.title: Borwein–Preiss Variational Principle
children.top_down_role: Smooth strengthened perturbation family.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a Banach space, \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and bounded below.
\(f(x_0)<\inf_X f+\varepsilon\), with \(\varepsilon>0\), \(\lambda>0\), and \(p>1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A nearby point is a strict minimizer after addition of a differentiable series of power-distance perturbations.

notation.meaning: Power used in the smooth perturbation
Perturbation centers converging to the minimizer

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Power-distance form of the Borwein–Preiss smooth variational principle on a Banach space.

source_refs.locator: 2.3.3 Smooth Variational Principles p. 210
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
There exist \(\bar x\in X\), points \(x_i\to\bar x\), and numbers \(\mu_i>0\) with \(\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}\mu_i=1\), such that \(\|\bar x-x_0\|<\lambda\), \(f(\bar x)\leq f(x_0)\), and \(\bar x\) is a strict global minimizer of
\[
x\longmapsto f(x)+\frac{\varepsilon}{\lambda^p}\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}\mu_i\|x-x_i\|^p.
\]
For \(p>1\), the perturbation is Fréchet differentiable at \(\bar x\) whenever the norm-power terms have the required smoothness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A near-minimizer can be moved slightly so that a convergent weighted sum of smooth power-distance penalties makes it a strict minimizer.
knowledge_statements.title: Borwein–Preiss Variational Principle

children.title: Deville–Godefroy–Zizler Variational Principle
children.top_down_role: Smooth variational principle for Banach-space renorming structures.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a Banach space admitting a \(C^1\)-smooth Lipschitz bump function.
\(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and bounded below.
\(\varepsilon>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An arbitrarily small smooth Lipschitz perturbation makes \(f\) attain a strong minimum.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: DGZ smooth variational principle in a Banach space possessing a smooth Lipschitz bump.

source_refs.locator: 2.3.3 Smooth Variational Principles p. 210
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
There exists a bounded \(C^1\)-smooth Lipschitz function \(g:X\to\mathbb R\) satisfying
\[
\|g\|_\infty<\varepsilon,
\qquad
\sup_{x\in X}\|g'(x)\|<\varepsilon,
\]
such that \(f+g\) has a strong minimum at some \(\bar x\in X\); that is, \((f+g)(x_n)\to(f+g)(\bar x)\) implies \(x_n\to\bar x\). The differentiability class of \(g\) may be raised when the available bump function has the corresponding higher smoothness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Banach space with a smooth Lipschitz bump permits arbitrarily small smooth perturbations that force lower-semicontinuous objectives to have strong minima.
knowledge_statements.title: Deville–Godefroy–Zizler Variational Principle

children.title: Smooth-Bump Perturbation Principles
children.top_down_role: Perturbation families controlled by smooth bump functions.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a Banach space with a bounded \(C^1\)-smooth Lipschitz bump.
\(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and bounded below.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Smooth bump functions generate perturbations that are simultaneously small in value and derivative and that enforce minimization.

source_refs.locator: 2.3.3 Smooth Variational Principles p. 210

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(\eta>0\), the smooth-bump perturbation mechanism produces a bounded \(C^1\)-smooth Lipschitz function \(g:X\to\mathbb R\) with
\[
\sup_{x\in X}|g(x)|<\eta,
\qquad
\sup_{x\in X}\|g'(x)\|<\eta,
\]
for which \(f+g\) attains a minimum. At any minimizer \(\bar x\), the smooth sum rule yields \(-g'(\bar x)\in\widehat\partial f(\bar x)\), so the perturbation controls both objective displacement and first-order residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Smooth bumps yield perturbations whose values and derivatives are uniformly small, while forcing a minimizer and a controlled subgradient residual.

children.title: Fuzzy Subdifferential Principles
children.top_down_role: Approximate generalized-gradient localization.

knowledge_statements.title: Fuzzy Subdifferential Principles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fuzzy Fréchet-subdifferential stationarity for a finite sum on an Asplund space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exist \(x_i\in X\) and \(x_i^*\in\widehat\partial f_i(x_i)\) such that
\[
\|x_i-\bar x\|<\varepsilon,
\qquad
|f_i(x_i)-f_i(\bar x)|<\varepsilon,
\qquad
\left\|\sum_{i=1}^m x_i^*\right\|<\varepsilon.
\]
Thus exact stationarity of the sum is represented, up to an arbitrarily small residual, by subgradients evaluated at possibly different nearby points rather than necessarily at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a local minimum of a nonsmooth sum, nearby Fréchet subgradients of the summands can be chosen so their sum is arbitrarily small.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is an Asplund space and \(f_i:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), \(1\leq i\leq m\), are lower semicontinuous near \(\bar x\).

knowledge_statements.title: Approximate Minimizers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global additive-gap definition of approximate minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A point \(x_\varepsilon\in\operatorname{dom}f\) is an \(\varepsilon\)-approximate global minimizer of \(f\) if
\[
f(x_\varepsilon)\leq\inf_{x\in X}f(x)+\varepsilon.
\]
For \(\varepsilon=0\), this is exact global minimization. For a nonempty feasible set \(C\subset X\), define its indicator by \(\delta_C(x)=0\) for \(x\in C\) and \(\delta_C(x)=+\infty\) otherwise. The constrained definition is obtained by replacing \(f\) with \(f+\delta_C\), equivalently by requiring \(x_\varepsilon\in C\) and taking the infimum over \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An approximate minimizer is a feasible point whose objective value exceeds the global infimum by no more than the prescribed tolerance.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a nonempty set and \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and bounded below.
\(\varepsilon\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_\varepsilon\) is an \(\varepsilon\)-approximate minimizer exactly when its objective gap is at most \(\varepsilon\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The point \(x\) is \(\eta\)-stationary for \(f\), relative to \(\partial\), when
\[
\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial f(x))\leq\eta.
\]
Equivalently, \(0\in\overline{\partial f(x)+\eta B_{X^*}}\). If \(\partial f(x)\) is norm closed and the distance is attained, this reduces to the existence of \(x^*\in\partial f(x)\) satisfying \(\|x^*\|\leq\eta\). Exact stationarity corresponds to \(\eta=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point is approximately stationary when its generalized subdifferential comes within the chosen tolerance of the zero dual vector.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
There exists \(\bar x\in X\) such that
\[
d(\bar x,x_0)\leq\lambda,
\qquad
f(\bar x)\leq f(x_0),
\qquad
f(x)>f(\bar x)-\frac{\varepsilon}{\lambda}d(x,\bar x)
\quad\text{for all }x\neq\bar x.
\]
Consequently, the strong slope satisfies \(|\nabla f|(\bar x)\leq\varepsilon/\lambda\). In Banach-space settings where an applicable subdifferential slope estimate holds, this yields a corresponding approximate subdifferential stationarity condition at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Ekeland’s principle converts an objective gap into a nearby point whose metric slope is bounded by the gap divided by the localization radius.

children.title: Localization-Loss Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Regimes where near-optimality does not yield useful local stationarity.

assumptions_latex: \(X=\mathbb R\) and \(f(x)=e^x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Near-optimality and vanishing first-order residual do not imply localization when compactness or coercivity is absent.
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete loss of localization without coercivity or compact sublevel sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The smooth convex function \(f(x)=e^x\) satisfies \(\inf_{x\in\mathbb R}f(x)=0\), but it has no minimizer. For \(x_n=-n\),
\[
f(x_n)=e^{-n}\downarrow0,
\qquad
\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial f(x_n))=|f'(x_n)|=e^{-n}\downarrow0,
\qquad
|x_n|\to\infty.
\]
Thus the same sequence is increasingly near-optimal and approximately stationary while escaping every bounded set. A coercivity, compactness, or independent localization hypothesis is therefore necessary to infer a convergent localized subsequence from these two residuals alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the exponential function, near-minimizers have vanishing gradients but escape to minus infinity, so stationarity does not supply localization without compactness or coercivity.
knowledge_statements.title: Localization-Loss Boundaries

For every \(x_0\in\operatorname{dom}f\) and every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exists \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\) such that
\[
\|x-x_0\|<\varepsilon,

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((X,d)\) be a metric space and let \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and bounded below. The minimization problem \(\inf_{x\in X}f(x)\) is variationally well-posed in the Tikhonov sense when there exists a unique minimizer \(\bar x\in X\) and every minimizing sequence converges to it; explicitly, whenever \(f(x_k)\to\inf_X f\), one has \(d(x_k,\bar x)\to0\). Equivalently, the approximate solution sets \(\{x:f(x)\le\inf_X f+\varepsilon\}\) shrink to \(\bar x\) as \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A problem is variationally well-posed when it has one minimizer and every sequence approaching the optimal value converges to that minimizer.

children.top_down_role: Exceptional regimes exhibiting nonuniqueness or unstable minimizers.

assumptions_latex: For \(p\in\mathbb R\), define \(f_p(x)=x^4-px^2\) on \(\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The minimizer is unique for \(p\le0\), while \(\operatorname*{argmin}f_p=\{-\sqrt{p/2},\sqrt{p/2}\}\) for \(p>0\); hence \(p=0\) is a boundary of uniqueness stability.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bifurcation example marking loss of uniqueness under arbitrarily small perturbations.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 4. Characterizations of Well-Posedness and Sensitivity Analysis p. 377
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(p\in\mathbb R\), consider \(f_p(x)=x^4-px^2\) on \(\mathbb R\). If \(p\le0\), then \(x=0\) is the unique global minimizer. If \(p>0\), then \[\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathbb R}f_p(x)=\left\{-\sqrt{p/2},\sqrt{p/2}\right\}.\] Consequently, every neighborhood of \(p=0\) contains parameters with a unique minimizer and parameters with two minimizers. The parameter \(p=0\) is therefore an instability boundary for uniqueness and single-valued solution selection, despite continuous dependence of the minimizing set in a weaker set-valued sense.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quartic family changes from one minimizer to two across zero, making zero a sharp boundary for uniqueness-based stability.
knowledge_statements.title: Instability Boundaries

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 4. Characterizations of Well-Posedness and Sensitivity Analysis p. 377

children.title: Perturbational Applicability Boundary
children.top_down_role: Ambient-space and function-class boundaries for perturbational principles.

children.title: Incomplete Metric Spaces
children.top_down_role: Failure boundary for complete-metric-space principles.

assumptions_latex: \(X=(0,1)\) with the Euclidean metric.
\(f:X\to\mathbb R\) is defined by \(f(x)=x\).
\(\varepsilon=1/2\), \(\lambda=1\), and \(x_0=1/4\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Although \(f(x_0)\le\inf_X f+\varepsilon\), no \(\bar x\in X\) satisfies \(f(\bar x)<f(x)+(\varepsilon/\lambda)|x-\bar x|\) for every \(x\in X\setminus\{\bar x\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete failure of Ekeland perturbed minimality without metric completeness.

source_refs.locator: 2.3 Relations with Variational Principles p. 203
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=(0,1)\) have the Euclidean metric, and define \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) by \(f(x)=x\). For \(\varepsilon=1/2\), \(\lambda=1\), and \(x_0=1/4\), one has \(f(x_0)\le\inf_X f+\varepsilon\). Nevertheless, there is no \(\bar x\in X\) such that \[f(\bar x)<f(x)+\frac{\varepsilon}{\lambda}|x-\bar x|\qquad\text{for every }x\in X\setminus\{\bar x\}.\] Hence the complete-space perturbed-minimality conclusion can fail on an incomplete metric space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On the incomplete open interval, the displayed approximate minimizer does not yield an Ekeland-type strict perturbed minimizer.
knowledge_statements.title: Incomplete Metric Spaces

source_witnesses.locator: 2.3 Relations with Variational Principles p. 203
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

children.title: Closure-Relaxation Repair Boundary
children.top_down_role: Models requiring closure or relaxation before perturbation.

children.title: Nonclosed Models
children.top_down_role: Feasible-domain failures caused by missing closure.

assumptions_latex: \(X=\mathbb R\), \(C=(0,1)\), and \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) is defined by \(f(x)=x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{x\in C}f(x)=0\) and \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x)=\varnothing\), whereas \(0\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\overline C}f(x)\) for \(\overline C=[0,1]\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Attainment failure caused by a nonclosed feasible model and its closure repair.

source_refs.locator: 1.1.5 Variational Descriptions and Minimality p. 33
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=\mathbb R\), let \(C=(0,1)\), and define \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) by \(f(x)=x\). Then \[\inf_{x\in C}f(x)=0,\qquad \operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x)=\varnothing.\] For the closed enlargement \(\overline C=[0,1]\), one has \[0\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\overline C}f(x).\] Thus nonclosedness causes attainment failure in the original model, while passage to the closure restores attainment by enlarging the feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The continuous objective does not attain its infimum on the nonclosed feasible interval, while its closed enlargement admits a minimizer.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonclosed Models

source_witnesses.locator: 1.1.5 Variational Descriptions and Minimality p. 33
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

children.title: Non-Lower-Semicontinuous Models
children.top_down_role: Objective failures caused by downward jumps under limits.

assumptions_latex: \((X,d)=(\mathbb R,|\cdot|)\) is complete.
\(0<\varepsilon<1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No point satisfies the stated strict perturbational minimality inequality.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete failure of an Ekeland-type conclusion without lower semicontinuity.

source_refs.locator: 2.3 Relations with Variational Principles p. 203
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(f\) is bounded below and satisfies \(\inf_{\mathbb R}f=0\), but it is not lower semicontinuous at \(0\). For every \(0<\varepsilon<1\), there is no \(\bar x\in\mathbb R\) such that \(f(\bar x)\le \inf_{\mathbb R} f+\varepsilon\) and \(f(x)>f(\bar x)-\varepsilon|x-\bar x|\) for every \(x\ne\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded-below but non-lower-semicontinuous function on a complete space can fail the strict perturbational minimum conclusion of Ekeland's principle.
knowledge_statements.title: Non-Lower-Semicontinuous Models

source_witnesses.locator: 2.3 Relations with Variational Principles p. 203
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

children.title: Closure Repair Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Passage to closed feasible structures before perturbation.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a topological space and \(g:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is extended-real-valued.
\(\operatorname{cl}g\) is the greatest lower-semicontinuous function majorized by \(g\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The repaired problem is exact precisely when its value and relevant minimizers transfer back to \(g\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Epigraphical closure as a repair interface for nonclosed models.

source_refs.locator: 6.1.2 Bolza Problem for Differential Inclusions and Relaxation Stability p. 168
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Closure repair replaces \(g\) by its lower-semicontinuous envelope \(\operatorname{cl}g\), characterized by \(\operatorname{epi}(\operatorname{cl}g)=\overline{\operatorname{epi}g}\) whenever the epigraph closure is itself an epigraph. One always has \(\operatorname{cl}g\le g\), hence \(\inf_X\operatorname{cl}g\le\inf_X g\). The interface is value-exact when equality holds; a repaired minimizer \(\bar x\) solves the original problem whenever additionally \(g(\bar x)=\operatorname{cl}g(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Epigraphical closure produces a lower-semicontinuous model; value equality and equality at a repaired minimizer determine whether the repair transfers back.
knowledge_statements.title: Closure Repair Interfaces

source_witnesses.locator: 6.1.2 Bolza Problem for Differential Inclusions and Relaxation Stability p. 168
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation II

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The closure interface is mathematically plausible, and property is a reasonable role, but the cited locator concerns relaxation stability for differential inclusions rather than the asserted general topological epigraph-closure construction. A source directly treating lower-semicontinuous envelopes and epigraphical closure is required.

children.title: Relaxation Repair Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Passage to lower-semicontinuous objective representations before perturbation.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a metric space and \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper.
\(\bar f\) is the sequential lower-semicontinuous envelope of \(f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Relaxation is exact when \(\inf_X\bar f=\inf_X f\), with recovery sequences connecting relaxed and original models.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential lower-semicontinuous relaxation and its exactness interface.

source_refs.locator: 6.1.2 Bolza Problem for Differential Inclusions and Relaxation Stability p. 168
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The sequential relaxation of \(f\) is represented by \[\bar f(x)=\inf\left\{\liminf_{n\to\infty}f(x_n):x_n\to x\right\}.\] It is lower semicontinuous and satisfies \(\bar f\le f\). There is no relaxation gap precisely when \(\inf_X\bar f=\inf_X f\). A relaxed minimizer \(\bar x\) is approximable without value loss when a recovery sequence \(x_n\to\bar x\) exists with \(f(x_n)\to\bar f(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relaxation takes the best limiting cost along convergent sequences. Exactness means equal infima, while recovery sequences approximate relaxed minimizers without value loss.
knowledge_statements.title: Relaxation Repair Interfaces

source_witnesses.locator: 6.1.2 Bolza Problem for Differential Inclusions and Relaxation Stability p. 168
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation II

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation is standard on metric spaces and fits the relaxation-interface leaf, but the cited specialized Bolza-problem section does not reliably support the general sequential-envelope formula and recovery-sequence assertions. A direct relaxation or variational-analysis source is required.

children.title: Missing Smooth Perturbation Structure
children.top_down_role: Banach-space geometries lacking the structures required by smooth variants.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a Banach space.
The chosen smooth variational principle requires perturbations from a class \(\mathcal P\) of smooth Lipschitz bump-type functions.
\(X\) has no nonzero perturbation in \(\mathcal P\) with bounded support.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The hypotheses do not justify the corresponding smooth perturbational variational principle on \(X\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary for variants requiring smooth Lipschitz bump perturbations.

source_refs.locator: 2.3.3 Smooth Variational Principles p. 210
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A smooth variational principle that constructs \(g\in\mathcal P\) with prescribed small norm and derivative bounds requires the ambient Banach geometry to supply such perturbations. If \(X\) admits no nonzero smooth Lipschitz bump of the required differentiability class, that construction cannot be invoked. Completeness of \(X\) alone still supports nonsmooth metric perturbations, but it does not imply the missing smooth perturbation conclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Completeness alone does not supply smooth bump perturbations. Smooth variational principles requiring them are unavailable in Banach geometries lacking the specified bump-function structure.
knowledge_statements.title: Missing Smooth Perturbation Structure

children.title: Applicable Ambient-Space Regimes
children.top_down_role: Metric and topological settings supporting perturbational principles.

assumptions_latex: \((X,d)\) is a complete metric space.
\(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and bounded below.
\(f(x_0)\le\inf_X f+\varepsilon\) with \(\varepsilon>0\) and \(\lambda>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists \(\bar x\) satisfying the Ekeland perturbational minimality conclusions.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complete-metric-space form of Ekeland’s variational principle.

source_refs.locator: 2.3 Relations with Variational Principles p. 203
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: There exists \(\bar x\in X\) such that \(f(\bar x)\le f(x_0)\), \(d(\bar x,x_0)\le\lambda\), and \[f(x)>f(\bar x)-\frac{\varepsilon}{\lambda}d(x,\bar x)\qquad\text{for every }x\ne\bar x.\] Thus the metric perturbation form requires completeness but no linear, normed, finite-dimensional, or smooth structure on the ambient space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Ekeland’s principle applies on every complete metric space: a near-minimizer becomes a strict minimizer after adding a small metric-distance perturbation.
knowledge_statements.title: Applicable Ambient-Space Regimes

source_witnesses.locator: 2.3 Relations with Variational Principles p. 203
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

children.title: Applicable Function-Class Regimes
children.top_down_role: Objective classes compatible with perturbational conclusions.

assumptions_latex: \((X,d)\) is a complete metric space.
\(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and bounded below.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every sufficiently accurate approximate minimizer admits the standard Ekeland perturbational refinement.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard objective class for the metric perturbational principle.

source_refs.locator: 2.3 Relations with Variational Principles p. 203
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The applicable function-class predicate is \(\operatorname{dom}f\ne\varnothing\), \(\inf_X f> -\infty\), and \[f(x)\le\liminf_{n\to\infty}f(x_n)\quad\text{whenever }x_n\to x.\] Under this predicate, for every \(x_0\in\operatorname{dom}f\) with \(f(x_0)\le\inf_X f+\varepsilon\) and every \(\lambda>0\), Ekeland’s perturbational conclusion applies. Convexity, differentiability, and finite-valuedness are unnecessary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The standard metric principle covers proper, lower-semicontinuous, bounded-below extended-real functions; it requires neither convexity nor differentiability.
knowledge_statements.title: Applicable Function-Class Regimes

knowledge_statements.statement_title: First-order optimality for a differentiable–convex composite problem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates the generally necessary local condition from its necessary-and-sufficient convex specialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{E}\to(-\infty,\infty]\) be proper and let \(g:\mathbb{E}\to(-\infty,\infty]\) be proper and convex, with \(\operatorname{dom}g\subseteq\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)\). For \((P):\min_{x\in\mathbb{E}} f(x)+g(x)\): (a) if \(x^*\in\operatorname{dom}g\) is a local minimizer and \(f\) is differentiable at \(x^*\), then \(-\nabla f(x^*)\in\partial g(x^*)\); (b) if, in addition, \(f\) is convex and differentiable at \(x^*\in\operatorname{dom}g\), then \(x^*\) is a global minimizer of \((P)\) if and only if \(-\nabla f(x^*)\in\partial g(x^*)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A local minimizer of a differentiable-plus-convex composite objective satisfies composite stationarity. If the differentiable term is also convex, that condition is equivalent to global optimality.
assumptions_latex: f:\mathbb{E}\to(-\infty,\infty]\text{ is proper}
g:\mathbb{E}\to(-\infty,\infty]\text{ is proper and convex}
\operatorname{dom}g\subseteq\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)
x^*\in\operatorname{dom}g
f\text{ is differentiable at }x^*
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^*\text{ local minimizer}\Rightarrow-\nabla f(x^*)\in\partial g(x^*);\qquad f\text{ convex}\Rightarrow\bigl[x^*\text{ global minimizer}\Longleftrightarrow-\nabla f(x^*)\in\partial g(x^*)\bigr]

source_evidence.locator: Subgradients / Optimality Conditions / The Nonconvex Composite Model / Theorem 3.35

children.title: Smooth Fermat Rules
children.top_down_role: Differentiable unconstrained minimality.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a normed space and \(U\subset X\) is open.
\(f:U\to\mathbb R\) is Fréchet differentiable at \(\bar x\in U\).
\(\bar x\) is a local minimizer of \(f\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unconstrained Fréchet-differentiable Fermat rule on an open set.

source_refs.locator: C. Smooth Manifolds and Convex Sets p. 202
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(v\in X\), local minimality applied along \(t\mapsto\bar x+tv\) gives the necessary first-order condition \[Df(\bar x)[v]=0.\] Equivalently, the continuous linear functional \(Df(\bar x)\) is the zero element of \(X^*\). This conclusion is an unconstrained rule; at a boundary point of a feasible set, feasible-direction or normal-cone terms are required instead.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At an unconstrained local minimizer lying in an open domain, every Fréchet derivative direction vanishes; equivalently, the gradient functional is zero.
knowledge_statements.title: Smooth Fermat Rules

source_witnesses.locator: C. Smooth Manifolds and Convex Sets p. 202
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Fermat rule is mathematically standard, but the cited Rockafellar-Wets locator is a finite-dimensional source while the candidate asserts the result for an arbitrary normed space. The opening derivational sentence is also proof text. A source explicitly supporting the stated normed-space scope is required before a precise replacement can be accepted.

children.title: Convex Subgradient Fermat Rules
children.top_down_role: Convex subgradient minimality.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a real locally convex space and \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and convex.
\(\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bar x\in\operatorname{argmin}f\) if and only if \(0\in\partial f(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact global Fermat rule for proper convex functions.

source_refs.locator: Chapter II. Variational Inequalities in Hilbert Space p. 23
source_refs.source_title: An Introduction to Variational Inequalities and Their Applications

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The convex subdifferential is \[\partial f(\bar x)=\left\{x^*\in X^*:f(x)\ge f(\bar x)+\langle x^*,x-\bar x\rangle\ \text{for every }x\in X\right\}.\] Consequently, \(0\in\partial f(\bar x)\) holds exactly when \(f(x)\ge f(\bar x)\) for every \(x\in X\), which is equivalent to global minimality. Thus, for convex objectives, the subgradient Fermat condition is both necessary and sufficient.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a proper convex function, a point is a global minimizer exactly when zero belongs to its convex subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.title: Convex Subgradient Fermat Rules

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter II. Variational Inequalities in Hilbert Space p. 23
source_witnesses.source_title: An Introduction to Variational Inequalities and Their Applications

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The zero-subgradient characterization is correct under the stated definition, but the cited locator is specifically in a Hilbert-space chapter and does not establish the asserted arbitrary locally convex-space scope. The statement also includes a derivation rather than only the knowledge claim. A directly supporting convex-analysis source is required.

children.title: Generalized-Subdifferential Fermat Rules
children.top_down_role: Regular, limiting, proximal, and Clarke-type minimality.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional normed space and \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper.
\(\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}f\) is a local minimizer.
For the Clarke assertion, \(f\) is locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Zero belongs to each applicable generalized subdifferential at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional local-minimum inclusions for standard generalized subdifferentials.

source_refs.locator: 2.3.2 Subdifferential Variational Principles p. 206
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At a local minimizer \(\bar x\), the generalized Fermat inclusions are \(0\in\widehat\partial f(\bar x)\), \(0\in\partial_P f(\bar x)\), and \(0\in\partial f(\bar x)\). If \(f\) is locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\), then also \(0\in\partial_C f(\bar x)\). These are necessary conditions; without convexity, membership of zero alone generally does not imply local minimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a local minimum, zero lies in the regular, proximal, and limiting subdifferentials; for locally Lipschitz objectives it also lies in the Clarke subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.title: Generalized-Subdifferential Fermat Rules

source_witnesses.locator: 2.3.2 Subdifferential Variational Principles p. 206
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

children.title: Dini Directional Stationarity
children.top_down_role: One-sided directional regimes.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a normed space and \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\).
\(\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}f\) is a local minimizer and every ray \(\bar x+tv\) is locally admissible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f_D^-(\bar x;v)\ge0\) for every \(v\in X\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lower one-sided Dini stationarity for unconstrained local minima.

source_refs.locator: 8.2 Dini Stationarity p. 736
source_refs.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the lower Dini directional derivative by \[f_D^-(\bar x;v)=\liminf_{t\downarrow0}\frac{f(\bar x+tv)-f(\bar x)}{t}.\] Because \(\bar x\) is a local minimizer, the numerator is nonnegative for all sufficiently small \(t>0\). Hence \(f_D^-(\bar x;v)\ge0\) for every \(v\in X\). This necessary condition uses fixed directions and does not impose stability under perturbations of \(v\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At an unconstrained local minimum, every lower one-sided Dini directional derivative is nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.title: Dini Directional Stationarity

source_witnesses.locator: 8.2 Dini Stationarity p. 736
source_witnesses.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. II
