children.title: Hadamard Directional Stationarity
children.top_down_role: Directionally stable perturbation regimes.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional normed space and \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\).
\(\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}f\) is a local minimizer with a neighborhood contained in the effective domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f_H^-(\bar x;v)\ge0\) for every \(v\in X\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lower Hadamard stationarity, stable under perturbation of directions.

source_refs.locator: 4.1.1 Generalized directional derivatives p. 159
source_refs.source_title: Modern Nonconvex Nondifferentiable Optimization

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The lower Hadamard directional derivative is \[f_H^-(\bar x;v)=\liminf_{\substack{t\downarrow0\\w\to v}}\frac{f(\bar x+tw)-f(\bar x)}{t}.\] At a local minimizer \(\bar x\), one has \(f_H^-(\bar x;v)\ge0\) for every \(v\in X\). Unlike the fixed-direction Dini derivative, this stationarity condition tests directions \(w\) converging to \(v\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A local minimizer has nonnegative lower Hadamard derivatives in every direction, including along nearby directions converging to the tested direction.
knowledge_statements.title: Hadamard Directional Stationarity

source_witnesses.locator: 4.1.1 Generalized directional derivatives p. 159
source_witnesses.source_title: Modern Nonconvex Nondifferentiable Optimization

children.title: Bouligand Directional Stationarity
children.top_down_role: Contingent directional regimes for nonsmooth models.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional normed space, \(C\subset X\), and \(\bar x\in C\).
\(f:X\to\mathbb R\) is Hadamard directionally differentiable at \(\bar x\).
\(\bar x\) is a local minimizer of \(f\) over \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f'(\bar x;v)\ge0\) for every \(v\in T_C(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constrained Bouligand stationarity on the contingent tangent cone under directionally stable differentiability.

source_refs.locator: 4.1.1 Generalized directional derivatives p. 159
source_refs.source_title: Modern Nonconvex Nondifferentiable Optimization

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Bouligand contingent tangent cone is \[T_C(\bar x)=\left\{v\in X:\exists\,t_n\downarrow0,\ v_n\to v,\ \bar x+t_nv_n\in C\right\}.\] If \(f\) is Hadamard directionally differentiable at the constrained local minimizer \(\bar x\), then Bouligand stationarity holds: \[f'(\bar x;v)\ge0\qquad\text{for every }v\in T_C(\bar x).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a constrained local minimum, a Hadamard directionally differentiable objective has a nonnegative directional derivative along every direction in the Bouligand contingent tangent cone.
knowledge_statements.title: Bouligand Directional Stationarity

source_witnesses.locator: 4.1.1 Generalized directional derivatives p. 159
source_witnesses.source_title: Modern Nonconvex Nondifferentiable Optimization

children.title: Clarke Directional Stationarity
children.top_down_role: Convexified generalized-directional regimes.

assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is locally closed near \(\bar x\in C\).
\(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) is locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f^{\circ}(\bar x;d)\ge 0\quad\text{for every }d\in T_C^{\mathrm C}(\bar x)\).

notation.meaning: Clarke generalized directional derivative of f at x in direction d
Clarke tangent cone to C at x

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constrained Clarke directional stationarity for a locally Lipschitz objective in finite dimensions.

source_refs.locator: F. Tangent-Normal Relations p. 217
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A feasible point \(\bar x\) is Clarke directionally stationary for minimizing \(f\) over \(C\) when the Clarke generalized directional derivative is nonnegative along every Clarke-tangent direction:
\[
f^{\circ}(\bar x;d)\ge 0\qquad\text{for all }d\in T_C^{\mathrm C}(\bar x).
\]
This condition uses the robust, convexified tangent geometry and the upper generalized directional derivative; it does not assert nonnegativity of every more selective nonconvex directional derivative.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Clarke directional stationarity means that the Clarke generalized directional derivative is nonnegative in every Clarke-tangent direction.

children.title: Feasible-Direction Conditions
children.top_down_role: Minimality on directly realizable directions.

assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(\bar x\in C\).
\(f\) is differentiable at \(\bar x\), which is a local minimizer of \(f\) over \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\langle\nabla f(\bar x),d\rangle\ge 0\) for every \(d\in F_C(\bar x)\).

notation.meaning: Cone of directions whose short line segments from x remain feasible

knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order necessity along directly realizable straight-line directions.

source_refs.locator: F. Tangent-Normal Relations p. 217
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the feasible-direction cone by
\[
F_C(\bar x):=\left\{d\in\mathbb{R}^n:\text{there exists }\varepsilon>0\text{ such that }\bar x+td\in C\text{ for every }t\in[0,\varepsilon]\right\}.
\]
Local minimality and differentiability imply
\[
\langle\nabla f(\bar x),d\rangle\ge 0\qquad\text{for every }d\in F_C(\bar x).
\]
Thus no directly realizable direction is a strict first-order descent direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a differentiable local minimum, the gradient has nonnegative pairing with every direction whose sufficiently short forward segment remains feasible.
knowledge_statements.title: Feasible-Direction Conditions

children.title: Contingent-Tangent Conditions
children.top_down_role: Minimality on Bouligand tangent geometry.

assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(\bar x\in C\).
\(f\) is differentiable at \(\bar x\), which is a local minimizer of \(f\) over \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\langle\nabla f(\bar x),d\rangle\ge 0\) for every \(d\in T_C(\bar x)\).

notation.meaning: Bouligand or contingent tangent cone to C at x

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Bouligand-tangent necessary condition for a smooth objective.

source_refs.locator: F. Tangent-Normal Relations p. 217
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The contingent tangent cone is
\[
T_C(\bar x):=\left\{d:\text{there exist }t_k\downarrow0\text{ and }x_k\in C\text{ with }x_k\to\bar x\text{ and }(x_k-\bar x)/t_k\to d\right\}.
\]
If \(\bar x\) locally minimizes \(f\) on \(C\), then
\[
\langle\nabla f(\bar x),d\rangle\ge0\qquad\text{for all }d\in T_C(\bar x).
\]
Equivalently, the negative gradient belongs to the polar of the contingent tangent cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a smooth constrained local minimum, the gradient pairs nonnegatively with every Bouligand contingent-tangent direction.
knowledge_statements.title: Contingent-Tangent Conditions

children.title: Clarke-Tangent Conditions
children.top_down_role: Minimality on robust convexified tangent geometry.

assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is locally closed near \(\bar x\in C\).
\(f\) is differentiable at \(\bar x\), which is a local minimizer of \(f\) over \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\langle\nabla f(\bar x),d\rangle\ge 0\) for every \(d\in T_C^{\mathrm C}(\bar x)\).

notation.meaning: Clarke tangent cone to C at x

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Robust tangent condition using the Clarke cone in finite dimensions.

source_refs.locator: F. Tangent-Normal Relations p. 217
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A vector \(d\) belongs to \(T_C^{\mathrm C}(\bar x)\) when, for every sequence \(x_k\to\bar x\) with \(x_k\in C\) and every \(t_k\downarrow0\), there exist \(d_k\to d\) such that \(x_k+t_kd_k\in C\). Local minimality implies
\[
\langle\nabla f(\bar x),d\rangle\ge0\qquad\text{for every }d\in T_C^{\mathrm C}(\bar x).
\]
The cone is closed and convex, so this is a convexified robust first-order condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smooth local minimum has nonnegative gradient pairing with every robust Clarke-tangent direction.
knowledge_statements.title: Clarke-Tangent Conditions

children.title: Linearized-Cone Conditions
children.top_down_role: Minimality on constraint-generated tangent approximations.

assumptions_latex: \(C=\{x:g_i(x)\le0,\ i=1,\ldots,m;\ h_j(x)=0,\ j=1,\ldots,p\}\), with all functions continuously differentiable near \(\bar x\in C\).
\(f\) is differentiable at the local minimizer \(\bar x\).
Abadie's condition \(T_C(\bar x)=L_C(\bar x)\) holds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\langle\nabla f(\bar x),d\rangle\ge0\) for every \(d\in L_C(\bar x)\).

notation.meaning: Set of active inequality indices at x
Linearized cone of the constraint system at x
Contingent tangent cone to C at x

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth nonlinear constraints under Abadie's tangent-cone equality.

source_refs.locator: 5.1.2 Necessary Conditions under Operator Constraints p. 9
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(I(\bar x):=\{i:g_i(\bar x)=0\}\) and define
\[
L_C(\bar x):=\{d:\langle\nabla g_i(\bar x),d\rangle\le0\text{ for }i\in I(\bar x),\ \langle\nabla h_j(\bar x),d\rangle=0\text{ for all }j\}.
\]
The tangent condition and Abadie's equality yield
\[
\langle\nabla f(\bar x),d\rangle\ge0\qquad\text{for every }d\in L_C(\bar x).
\]
Without a condition ensuring \(L_C(\bar x)\subset T_C(\bar x)\), local minimality alone need not imply this stronger linearized-cone inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under Abadie's condition, a smooth local minimum has nonnegative gradient pairing with every direction satisfying the linearized active constraints.
knowledge_statements.title: Linearized-Cone Conditions

children.title: Convex-Normal Stationarity
children.top_down_role: Stationarity for convex feasible geometry.

assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty and convex, and \(\bar x\in C\).
\(f\) is differentiable at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(-\nabla f(\bar x)\in N_C^{\mathrm{cvx}}(\bar x)\).

notation.meaning: Convex-analysis normal cone to C at x

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth-objective stationarity over a convex feasible set.

source_refs.locator: B. Normal Cones and Clarke Regularity p. 199
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The convex normal cone is
\[
N_C^{\mathrm{cvx}}(\bar x):=\{v\in\mathbb{R}^n:\langle v,x-\bar x\rangle\le0\text{ for every }x\in C\}.
\]
Convex-normal stationarity is the inclusion
\[
-\nabla f(\bar x)\in N_C^{\mathrm{cvx}}(\bar x),
\]
equivalently \(\langle\nabla f(\bar x),x-\bar x\rangle\ge0\) for every \(x\in C\). Every local minimizer of the differentiable objective over the convex set satisfies this condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convex-normal stationarity places the negative gradient in the convex normal cone, equivalently giving a variational inequality over the feasible set.
knowledge_statements.title: Convex-Normal Stationarity

children.title: Regular-Normal Stationarity
children.top_down_role: Stationarity using regular normal geometry.

assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is locally closed near \(\bar x\in C\).
\(f\) is differentiable at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(-\nabla f(\bar x)\in\widehat N_C(\bar x)\).

notation.meaning: Fréchet or regular normal cone to C at x
Contingent tangent cone to C at x

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fréchet-normal stationarity for a smooth objective on a locally closed set.

source_refs.locator: B. Normal Cones and Clarke Regularity p. 199
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Regular-normal stationarity is
\[
-\nabla f(\bar x)\in\widehat N_C(\bar x),
\]
where
\[
\widehat N_C(\bar x):=\left\{v:\limsup_{\substack{x\to\bar x,\ x\in C\\x\ne\bar x}}\frac{\langle v,x-\bar x\rangle}{\|x-\bar x\|}\le0\right\}.
\]
Equivalently, \(\langle\nabla f(\bar x),d\rangle\ge0\) for every \(d\in T_C(\bar x)\). A differentiable local minimizer of \(f\) over \(C\) satisfies this inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Regular-normal stationarity places the negative gradient in the Fréchet normal cone; every smooth constrained local minimum satisfies it.
knowledge_statements.title: Regular-Normal Stationarity

children.title: Limiting-Normal Stationarity
children.top_down_role: Stationarity using nonconvex limiting normals.

assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is locally closed near \(\bar x\in C\).
\(f\) is differentiable at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(-\nabla f(\bar x)\in N_C(\bar x)\).

notation.meaning: Mordukhovich or limiting normal cone to C at x
Fréchet or regular normal cone to C at x

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mordukhovich-normal stationarity for nonconvex feasible geometry.

source_refs.locator: 2.5.2 Specific Normal and Subdifferential Structures p. 235
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The limiting normal cone is the outer limit
\[
N_C(\bar x):=\left\{v:\text{there exist }x_k\to\bar x,\ x_k\in C,\ v_k\to v,\ v_k\in\widehat N_C(x_k)\right\}.
\]
Limiting-normal stationarity is
\[
-\nabla f(\bar x)\in N_C(\bar x).
\]
Because \(\widehat N_C(\bar x)\subset N_C(\bar x)\), every differentiable local minimizer satisfies this inclusion, although the converse generally fails and the limiting cone can be nonconvex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Limiting-normal stationarity requires the negative gradient to be a limit of nearby regular normals, accommodating nonconvex feasible sets.
knowledge_statements.title: Limiting-Normal Stationarity

children.title: Clarke-Normal Stationarity
children.top_down_role: Stationarity using convexified normal geometry.

assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is locally closed near \(\bar x\in C\).
\(f\) is differentiable at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(-\nabla f(\bar x)\in N_C^{\mathrm C}(\bar x)\).

notation.meaning: Clarke normal cone to C at x
Clarke tangent cone to C at x
Negative polar of a cone K

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stationarity using the closed convex Clarke normal cone.

source_refs.locator: B. Normal Cones and Clarke Regularity p. 199
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The Clarke normal cone is the negative polar
\[
N_C^{\mathrm C}(\bar x):=\bigl(T_C^{\mathrm C}(\bar x)\bigr)^{\circ}=\{v:\langle v,d\rangle\le0\text{ for every }d\in T_C^{\mathrm C}(\bar x)\}.
\]
Clarke-normal stationarity is
\[
-\nabla f(\bar x)\in N_C^{\mathrm C}(\bar x).
\]
In finite dimensions this cone equals the closed convex hull of \(N_C(\bar x)\). Hence limiting-normal stationarity implies Clarke-normal stationarity, while the reverse implication can fail.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Clarke-normal stationarity places the negative gradient in the polar of the Clarke tangent cone, a convexified normal condition.
knowledge_statements.title: Clarke-Normal Stationarity

children.title: Indicator-Function Stationarity
children.top_down_role: Extended-real representation of constrained minimality.

assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is locally closed near \(\bar x\in C\).
\(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) is continuously differentiable near \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\in\partial(f+\delta_C)(\bar x)\iff-\nabla f(\bar x)\in N_C(\bar x)\).

notation.meaning: Indicator function of C, zero on C and positive infinity outside C

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-real encoding with the limiting subdifferential.

source_refs.locator: 2.5.2 Specific Normal and Subdifferential Structures p. 235
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(\delta_C(x)=0\) for \(x\in C\) and \(\delta_C(x)=+\infty\) otherwise. Then minimizing \(f\) over \(C\) is equivalent to unconstrained minimization of the extended-real function \(f+\delta_C\). The smooth sum rule and the indicator-normal identity give
\[
\partial(f+\delta_C)(\bar x)=\nabla f(\bar x)+N_C(\bar x).
\]
Consequently,
\[
0\in\partial(f+\delta_C)(\bar x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad-\nabla f(\bar x)\in N_C(\bar x).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding the feasible-set indicator converts constrained stationarity into unconstrained limiting-subdifferential stationarity and reproduces limiting-normal stationarity.
knowledge_statements.title: Indicator-Function Stationarity

children.title: Subdifferential Stationarity
children.top_down_role: First-order stationarity expressed through generalized subdifferentials.

assumptions_latex: \(\varphi:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and lower semicontinuous.
\(\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}\varphi\) is a local minimizer of \(\varphi\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\in\widehat\partial\varphi(\bar x)\subset\partial\varphi(\bar x)\).

notation.meaning: Effective domain of the extended-real function

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Fermat condition for a proper lower-semicontinuous extended-real function.

source_refs.locator: 2.5.2 Specific Normal and Subdifferential Structures p. 235

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Subdifferential stationarity for \(\varphi\) at \(\bar x\) is the inclusion
\[
0\in\partial\varphi(\bar x).
\]
If \(\bar x\) is a local minimizer, then directly from the regular-subgradient inequality,
\[
0\in\widehat\partial\varphi(\bar x).
\]
Since \(\widehat\partial\varphi(\bar x)\subset\partial\varphi(\bar x)\), every local minimizer is limiting-subdifferentially stationary. This is a necessary condition only; without additional structure, a stationary point need not be locally minimizing.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every finite-dimensional local minimizer has zero as a regular, and therefore limiting, subgradient; this stationarity condition is not sufficient in general.
knowledge_statements.title: Subdifferential Stationarity

knowledge_statements.title: Normal–Subdifferential Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact indicator-function correspondence for regular and limiting constructions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the indicator function \(\delta_C\), regular subgradients are exactly regular normals and limiting subgradients are exactly limiting normals:
\[
\widehat\partial\delta_C(\bar x)=\widehat N_C(\bar x),
\qquad
\partial\delta_C(\bar x)=N_C(\bar x).
\]
Thus normal-cone constructions for sets are represented by the corresponding subdifferential constructions for indicator functions, with the regular or limiting type preserved.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The regular and limiting subdifferentials of a set indicator equal, respectively, the regular and limiting normal cones to that set.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is locally closed near \(\bar x\in C\).
\(\delta_C\) is the extended-real indicator of \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat\partial\delta_C(\bar x)=\widehat N_C(\bar x)\) and \(\partial\delta_C(\bar x)=N_C(\bar x)\).

children.title: Convex First-Order Sufficiency
children.top_down_role: Global sufficiency in convex optimization.

assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty and convex.
\(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\) is convex and differentiable.
\(x^*\in C\) satisfies \(\langle\nabla f(x^*),x-x^*\rangle\geq0\) for every \(x\in C\).

auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Differentiable finite-dimensional convex formulation on a convex feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(x\in C\), convexity gives the first-order inequality \[f(x)\geq f(x^*)+\langle\nabla f(x^*),x-x^*\rangle.\] Consequently, if \(x^*\) satisfies the variational inequality \[\langle\nabla f(x^*),x-x^*\rangle\geq0\qquad\text{for all }x\in C,\] then \(f(x)\geq f(x^*)\) for every \(x\in C\), and hence \(x^*\) is a global minimizer of \(f\) over \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a differentiable convex objective on a convex set, satisfaction of the first-order variational inequality guarantees global optimality.
knowledge_statements.title: Convex First-Order Sufficiency

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict convexity on an arbitrary convex domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(f\) is strictly convex on \(C\) if, for every pair \(x,y\in C\) with \(x\neq y\) and every \(t\in(0,1)\), \[f\bigl(tx+(1-t)y\bigr)<t f(x)+(1-t)f(y).\] This condition strengthens ordinary convexity only along nondegenerate line segments; no differentiability is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function is strictly convex when its value at every nontrivial mixture of distinct points lies strictly below the corresponding mixture of values.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(f\) is \(\mu\)-strongly convex on \(C\) if, for all \(x,y\in C\) and \(t\in[0,1]\), \[f\bigl(tx+(1-t)y\bigr)\leq t f(x)+(1-t)f(y)-\frac{\mu}{2}t(1-t)\|x-y\|^2.\] Equivalently, \(x\mapsto f(x)-\frac{\mu}{2}\|x\|^2\) is convex on \(C\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(x_1,x_2\in C\) are global minimizers and \(x_1\neq x_2\), then strict convexity at their midpoint yields \[f\left(\frac{x_1+x_2}{2}\right)<\frac{f(x_1)+f(x_2)}{2}=\inf_{x\in C}f(x),\] which is incompatible with the definition of the infimum. Therefore a strictly convex function has at most one minimizer on a convex set; under the attainment assumption, it has exactly one.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Strong convexity gives, for every \(x\in C\), \[f(x)\geq f(x^*)+\langle\nabla f(x^*),x-x^*\rangle+\frac{\mu}{2}\|x-x^*\|^2.\] The variational inequality at \(x^*\) makes the inner-product term nonnegative. Hence \[f(x)-f(x^*)\geq\frac{\mu}{2}\|x-x^*\|^2\qquad\text{for all }x\in C.\] In particular, \(x^*\) is the unique global minimizer.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Pseudoconvexity means that, for all \(x,y\in C\), \[f(y)<f(x)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\langle\nabla f(x),y-x\rangle<0.\] If \(\nabla f(x^*)=0\), the consequent cannot hold for any \(y\in C\). Thus no \(y\in C\) can satisfy \(f(y)<f(x^*)\), and \(x^*\) is a global minimizer of \(f\) on \(C\).

\(x^*\in C\) satisfies \(\nabla f(x^*)=0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(f\) is invex with respect to \(\eta\), meaning that \[f(y)-f(x)\geq\langle\nabla f(x),\eta(y,x)\rangle\qquad\text{for all }x,y\in C.\] At a stationary point \(x^*\), substitution of \(x=x^*\) gives \[f(y)-f(x^*)\geq\langle0,\eta(y,x^*)\rangle=0\qquad\text{for all }y\in C.\] Therefore \(x^*\) is a global minimizer.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under pseudoconvexity, stationarity is globally sufficient: \[\nabla f(x^*)=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x).\] Equivalently, \[\{x\in C:\nabla f(x)=0\}\subseteq\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x).\] The inclusion need not be an equality when a global minimizer lies at a boundary or when differentiability or the open-domain convention is changed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pseudoconvexity ensures that every unconstrained stationary point is globally optimal.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete failure of first-order sufficiency without generalized convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=x^3\) on \(\mathbb{R}\). Then \(f\) is continuously differentiable and \[f'(0)=0,\] so \(0\) is stationary. Nevertheless, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), \[f(-\varepsilon)=-\varepsilon^3<0=f(0)<\varepsilon^3=f(\varepsilon).\] Thus \(0\) is not a local minimizer and hence not a global minimizer. Differentiability and first-order stationarity alone therefore do not imply sufficiency in nonconvex optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The function x cubed has zero derivative at zero, but zero is not a minimum, showing that stationarity alone is insufficient.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\{x\in\mathbb{R}:x^2\leq0\}=\{0\}\). Its Bouligand tangent cone is \[T_C(0)=\{0\}.\] For the smooth constraint \(g(x)=x^2\leq0\), the linearized cone is \[L_C(0)=\{d\in\mathbb{R}:g'(0)d\leq0\}=\mathbb{R},\] because \(g'(0)=0\). knowledge_statements.title: Geometric Constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed-set constraints represented by indicators and normal cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A geometric constraint requires \(x\in\Omega\), where \(X\) is a Banach space and \(\Omega\subset X\) is a prescribed closed set. Define \(\delta_\Omega:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) by \(\delta_\Omega(x)=0\) for \(x\in\Omega\) and \(\delta_\Omega(x)=+\infty\) otherwise. For every proper function \(\varphi:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), \[\inf_{x\in\Omega}\varphi(x)=\inf_{x\in X}\bigl(\varphi(x)+\delta_\Omega(x)\bigr).\] Generalized derivatives of \(\delta_\Omega\) define the corresponding normal cone \(N_\Omega\), with the precise cone determined by the selected generalized-derivative construction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Membership in a closed feasible set can be encoded by its indicator function without changing the infimum. The chosen generalized derivative of that indicator determines the corresponding normal cone.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a Banach space and \(\Omega\subset X\) is closed.
\(\varphi:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{x\in\Omega}\varphi(x)=\inf_{x\in X}\bigl(\varphi(x)+\delta_\Omega(x)\bigr)\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-real functional equalities and inequalities on a Banach space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a Banach space, let \(I\) and \(E\) be disjoint finite index sets, and let \(\phi_k:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be given for every \(k\in I\cup E\). The associated functional constraint system has feasible set \[C:=\{x\in X:\phi_i(x)\leq0\ \text{for every }i\in I,\quad \phi_j(x)=0\ \text{for every }j\in E\}.\] Extended values allow domain restrictions to be incorporated into the constraint functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A functional constraint system imposes scalar inequalities indexed by I and scalar equalities indexed by E. Extended-real constraint functions may also encode domain restrictions.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a Banach space.
\(I\) and \(E\) are disjoint finite index sets.
For every \(k\in I\cup E\), \(\phi_k:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is an extended-real-valued function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C=\{x\in X:\phi_i(x)\leq0\ \forall i\in I,\ \phi_j(x)=0\ \forall j\in E\}\).

notation.meaning: constraint function indexed by an element of the union of the index sets

children.title: Composite Constraints
children.top_down_role: Constraints with nested mappings or compositionally structured terms.

assumptions_latex: \(X=\mathbb{R}^n\), \(Y=\mathbb{R}^m\).
\(F:X\to Y\) and \(D\subset Y\) is nonempty.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard inverse-image representation of a composite constraint
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional inverse-image formulation of a composite constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given a mapping \(F:X\to Y\) and a nonempty set \(D\subset Y\), the composite constraint generated by \((F,D)\) is
\[F(x)\in D.\]
Its feasible set and extended-real indicator representation are
\[C:=F^{-1}(D)=\{x\in X:F(x)\in D\},\qquad \delta_C(x)=\delta_D(F(x)),\]
where \(\delta_D(y)=0\) for \(y\in D\) and \(\delta_D(y)=+\infty\) otherwise. Thus minimizing an objective over \(C\) is equivalent, at the level of feasible minimizers, to minimizing its sum with \(\delta_D\circ F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A composite constraint requires a mapping value to belong to a prescribed set; its feasible-set indicator is the composition of that set’s indicator with the mapping.
knowledge_statements.title: Composite Constraints

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is mathematically correct, internally consistent, and appropriate for the Composite Constraints leaf, but it has no citation with an inspectable locator. The standard-field rationale is insufficient to satisfy the statement-review citation requirement.

children.title: Nonsmooth Constraint Systems
children.top_down_role: Constraint representations requiring generalized differential objects.

assumptions_latex: \(X=\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(Y=\mathbb{R}^m\).
\(G:X\to Y\) and \(Q:X\rightrightarrows Y\) are given mappings.

notation.meaning: Solution set of the generalized equation
Set-valued part of the constraint system

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generalized-equation representation of finite-dimensional nonsmooth constraints.

source_refs.locator: 5.2.2 Variational Systems as Equilibrium Constraints p. 51
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A finite-dimensional nonsmooth constraint system in generalized-equation form is
\[0\in G(x)+Q(x),\]
with solution set
\[S:=\{x\in X:0\in G(x)+Q(x)\}.\]
The set-valued mapping \(Q\) can encode nonsmooth or geometric restrictions. For example, if \(H:X\to Y\) and \(D\subset Y\) is nonempty, then the composite constraint \(H(x)\in D\) is equivalently written as
\[0\in H(x)+(-D).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite-dimensional nonsmooth constraint system can be represented by a generalized equation whose set-valued term encodes nonsmooth or geometric restrictions.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonsmooth Constraint Systems

children.title: Composite-Calculus Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Multiplier representations shaped by compositional structure.

assumptions_latex: \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) is continuously differentiable near \(\bar x\).
\(g:\mathbb{R}^m\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and lower semicontinuous, with \(g(F(\bar x))<+\infty\).
\(\partial^\infty g(F(\bar x))\cap\ker \nabla F(\bar x)^\top=\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial(g\circ F)(\bar x)\subseteq \nabla F(\bar x)^\top\partial g(F(\bar x))\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard limiting-subdifferential chain rule under a horizon qualification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limiting-subdifferential chain rule for a smooth inner mapping at a finite composite value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be continuously differentiable near \(\bar x\), and let \(g:\mathbb{R}^m\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and lower semicontinuous with \(g(F(\bar x))<+\infty\). If
\[\partial^\infty g(F(\bar x))\cap\ker \nabla F(\bar x)^\top=\{0\},\]
then
\[\partial(g\circ F)(\bar x)\subseteq \nabla F(\bar x)^\top\partial g(F(\bar x)).\]
Thus every limiting subgradient in \(\partial(g\circ F)(\bar x)\) has the form \(\nabla F(\bar x)^\top y^*\) for some \(y^*\in\partial g(F(\bar x))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a finite composite value, the horizon qualification gives the limiting-subdifferential chain-rule inclusion and an adjoint multiplier representation.
knowledge_statements.title: Composite-Calculus Interfaces

children.title: Separation Principles
children.top_down_role: Convex-geometric separation routes to dual certificates.

assumptions_latex: \(A,B\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) are nonempty, disjoint, and convex.
\(A\) is compact and \(B\) is closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists u\ne0,\alpha\in\mathbb{R}:\sup_{a\in A}\langle u,a\rangle<\alpha<\inf_{b\in B}\langle u,b\rangle\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: finite-dimensional strong separation theorem for a compact convex set and a disjoint closed convex set
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong separation in finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A,B\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty disjoint convex sets, with \(A\) compact and \(B\) closed. Then there exist \(u\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\}\) and \(\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\) such that
\[\sup_{a\in A}\langle u,a\rangle<\alpha<\inf_{b\in B}\langle u,b\rangle.\]
Thus the affine hyperplane \(\{x:\langle u,x\rangle=\alpha\}\) strictly separates the two sets. The vector \(u\) supplies a nonzero dual direction from which multiplier or infeasibility certificates may be constructed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Disjoint convex sets are strictly separable when one is compact and the other closed, producing a nonzero dual separating direction.
knowledge_statements.title: Separation Principles

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-dimensional strong-separation theorem is correctly stated, its hypotheses are sufficient, and theorem is the appropriate content kind. No source citation or inspectable locator is supplied.

children.title: Alternative Principles
children.top_down_role: Mutually exclusive primal-feasibility and dual-certificate systems.

assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) and \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{Exactly one of }\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax=b,\ x\ge 0\}\ne\varnothing\text{ and }\{y\in\mathbb{R}^m:A^\top y\ge 0,\ b^\top y<0\}\ne\varnothing\text{ holds.}\)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Farkas alternative for equality constraints with nonnegative variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) and \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\), exactly one of the following systems is solvable:
\[Ax=b,\qquad x\in\mathbb{R}^n,\qquad x\ge0,\]
or
\[A^\top y\ge0,\qquad b^\top y<0,\qquad y\in\mathbb{R}^m.\]
All vector inequalities are componentwise. The second system is the alternative certificate for failure of the first system.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exactly one holds: the right-hand side is a nonnegative combination of the matrix columns, or a dual vector strictly certifies that it is not.
knowledge_statements.title: Alternative Principles

children.title: Dual-Certificate Generation
children.top_down_role: Construction of multiplier candidates from convex-geometric certificates.

assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\), and \(y\in\mathbb{R}^m\).
\(A^\top y\ge0\) and \(b^\top y<0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}=\varnothing\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: directly checkable Farkas infeasibility certificate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional certificate for nonnegative linear feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) and \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\). A vector \(y\in\mathbb{R}^m\) satisfying
\[A^\top y\ge0,\qquad b^\top y<0\]
is a dual certificate that
\[\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}=\varnothing.\]
The certificate is directly checkable from the two displayed inequalities and is generated by the corresponding Farkas alternative whenever the primal system is infeasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vector with nonnegative transpose product and negative pairing with the right-hand side is a directly checkable certificate of infeasibility for a nonnegative linear system.
knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Certificate Generation

children.title: Separation Failure Regimes
children.top_down_role: Nonconvex or nonclosed settings limiting classical separation routes.

assumptions_latex: \(A=\{(s,t)\in\mathbb{R}^2:t\ge e^s\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\cap B=\varnothing\), \(\operatorname{dist}(A,B)=0\), and no affine hyperplane strongly separates \(A\) and \(B\) with a positive margin.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: explicit zero-distance closed-convex example showing failure of positive-margin separation without compactness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of positive-margin strong separation for unbounded closed convex sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The sets
\[A:=\{(s,t)\in\mathbb{R}^2:t\ge e^s\},\qquad B:=\{(s,0):s\in\mathbb{R}\}\]
are nonempty, closed, convex, disjoint, and unbounded, and they satisfy
\[\operatorname{dist}(A,B)=0.\]
They admit no affine-hyperplane separation with a positive strict margin. This is a failure boundary for the compact-versus-closed strong-separation theorem when compactness is removed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two disjoint unbounded closed convex sets can have zero distance and fail to admit affine-hyperplane separation with a positive strict margin.
knowledge_statements.title: Separation Failure Regimes

children.title: Normal-Cone Calculus Mechanisms
children.top_down_role: Generation through normals to intersections and inverse images.

assumptions_latex: \(C_1,\ldots,C_p\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) are closed convex and \(\bigcap_i\operatorname{ri}C_i\ne\varnothing\).
\(D\subset\mathbb{R}^m\) is closed convex, \(F(x)=Ax+b\), and \(F(\bar x)\in D\).
\(A\mathbb{R}^n\cap\operatorname{ri}(D-F(\bar x))\ne\varnothing\) for the inverse-image formula.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\cap_iC_i}(\bar x)=\sum_iN_{C_i}(\bar x)\) and \(N_{F^{-1}(D)}(\bar x)=A^\top N_D(F(\bar x))\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard qualified convex normal-cone rules for intersections and affine inverse images
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Qualified convex normal-cone calculus in finite dimensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(\bar x\in\bigcap_{i=1}^p C_i\), the relative-interior qualification \(\bigcap_{i=1}^p\operatorname{ri}C_i\ne\varnothing\) yields
\[N_{\cap_{i=1}^pC_i}(\bar x)=\sum_{i=1}^pN_{C_i}(\bar x).\]
For an affine mapping \(F(x)=Ax+b\), a closed convex set \(D\), and \(\bar x\in F^{-1}(D)\), the stated inverse-image qualification yields
\[N_{F^{-1}(D)}(\bar x)=A^\top N_D(F(\bar x)).\]
These identities generate normal multipliers for intersected constraints and composite affine constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under relative-interior qualifications, normals to intersections add, while normals to affine inverse images are adjoint images of normals to the target set.
knowledge_statements.title: Normal-Cone Calculus Mechanisms

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Both qualified convex normal-cone identities are mathematically consistent with the finite-dimensional role of this topic, and property is an acceptable kind for these calculus identities. The record lacks a source citation with a specific locator.

children.title: Extremal-Principle Mechanisms
children.top_down_role: Nonconvex multiplier generation through extremal set systems.

assumptions_latex: \(\Omega_1,\ldots,\Omega_p\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) are locally closed near \(\bar x\in\bigcap_i\Omega_i\).
The family \(\{\Omega_i\}_{i=1}^p\) is locally extremal at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists x_i^*\in N_{\Omega_i}(\bar x):\sum_i x_i^*=0,\ \sum_i\|x_i^*\|=1\).

notation.meaning: Limiting normal cone to a set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional limiting-normal form of the extremal principle.

source_refs.locator: 2.1.3 Extremal Principle in Finite Dimensions p. 178
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If the locally closed sets \(\Omega_1,\ldots,\Omega_p\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) form a locally extremal system at their common point \(\bar x\), then there exist limiting normals
\[x_i^*\in N_{\Omega_i}(\bar x),\qquad i=1,\ldots,p,\]
satisfying the balance and nontriviality conditions
\[\sum_{i=1}^p x_i^*=0,\qquad \sum_{i=1}^p\|x_i^*\|=1.\]
Thus local geometric extremality produces a normalized family of nonzero dual objects without requiring convexity of the sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local extremality of a finite nonconvex set system generates normalized limiting normals whose sum is zero.
knowledge_statements.title: Extremal-Principle Mechanisms

children.title: Constraint-Regularity Mechanisms
children.top_down_role: Multiplier generation from stability properties of constraint systems.

assumptions_latex: \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\), \(D\subset\mathbb{R}^m\), and \(C=\{x:F(x)\in D\}\).
\(\bar x\in C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dist}(x,C)\le\kappa\operatorname{dist}(F(x),D)\) locally for some \(\kappa>0\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard metric-subregularity error-bound condition for a composite constraint
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local error-bound form of constraint regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The composite constraint \(F(x)\in D\) is metrically subregular at the feasible point \(\bar x\) if there exist \(\kappa>0\) and a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\) such that
\[\operatorname{dist}(x,C)\le\kappa\operatorname{dist}(F(x),D)\qquad\text{for every }x\in U,\]
where \(C:=F^{-1}(D)\). This condition quantitatively converts residual size in the image space into distance from feasibility and is the regularity mechanism used in local penalty estimates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Constraint regularity is expressed by a local error bound that controls distance to feasibility by the constraint residual.
knowledge_statements.title: Constraint-Regularity Mechanisms

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The local error-bound inequality is a correct finite-dimensional metric-subregularity condition and fits the Constraint-Regularity Mechanisms leaf. No source citation with a specific locator is provided.

children.title: Exact-Penalty Mechanisms
children.top_down_role: Multiplier generation through locally exact penalized formulations.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\), \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\), and \(D\subset\mathbb{R}^m\) is nonempty.
\(C:=F^{-1}(D)\), and \(\bar x\in C\) is a local minimizer of \(f\) over \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists\bar\rho\ge0\ \exists U\ni\bar x\ \forall\rho\ge\bar\rho\ \forall x\in U:\ P_\rho(\bar x)\le P_\rho(x)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard local exact-penalty definition using the distance residual
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local distance-penalty exactness for composite constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define
\[P_\rho(x):=f(x)+\rho\operatorname{dist}(F(x),D),\qquad \rho\ge0.\]
This penalty is locally exact at the feasible constrained local minimizer \(\bar x\) if there exist \(\bar\rho\ge0\) and a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\) such that, for every \(\rho\ge\bar\rho\),
\[P_\rho(\bar x)\le P_\rho(x)\qquad\text{for every }x\in U.\]
The infimum of all admissible thresholds \(\bar\rho\) is the local exact-penalty parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A residual penalty is locally exact at a constrained local minimizer when every sufficiently large penalty parameter makes that point a local minimizer of the penalized objective.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact-Penalty Mechanisms

children.title: Regularity-to-Penalty Transfer
children.top_down_role: Connections between constraint stability and penalty exactness.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\), \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\), \(D\subset\mathbb{R}^m\) is nonempty, and \(C:=F^{-1}(D)\).
\(\bar x\in C\) is a local minimizer of \(f\) over \(C\), and \(C\) is locally closed at \(\bar x\).
\(f\) is locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\) with constant \(L\ge0\).
\(\operatorname{dist}(x,C)\le\kappa\operatorname{dist}(F(x),D)\) locally near \(\bar x\) for some \(\kappa>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\forall\rho>L\kappa:\ \bar x\text{ locally minimizes }x\mapsto f(x)+\rho\operatorname{dist}(F(x),D).\)

notation.meaning: Local Lipschitz constant of the objective

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard transfer from a local error bound and objective Lipschitz continuity to distance-penalty exactness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative transfer from metric subregularity to local exact penalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\), let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\), let \(D\subset\mathbb{R}^m\) be nonempty, and set \(C:=F^{-1}(D)\). Suppose \(\bar x\in C\) is a local minimizer of \(f\) over \(C\), the set \(C\) is locally closed at \(\bar x\), and \(f\) is locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\) with constant \(L\ge0\). If, for some \(\kappa>0\),
\[\operatorname{dist}(x,C)\le\kappa\operatorname{dist}(F(x),D)\]
holds locally near \(\bar x\), then for every \(\rho>L\kappa\), the point \(\bar x\) is a local minimizer of
\[x\longmapsto f(x)+\rho\operatorname{dist}(F(x),D).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a locally Lipschitz objective, a local constraint error bound transfers a constrained local minimum to the distance-penalized problem whenever the penalty parameter exceeds the product of the two moduli.
knowledge_statements.title: Regularity-to-Penalty Transfer

children.title: Penalty-Exactness Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Regimes where penalization fails to preserve local solutions.

assumptions_latex: \(f\) is locally Lipschitz near a feasible local minimizer \(\bar x\).
The feasible set \(S\) satisfies \(d(x,S)\leq \kappa r(x)\) locally, where \(r\geq0\) vanishes exactly on \(S\).
\(f\) has local Lipschitz modulus at most \(L\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bar x\) locally minimizes \(f(x)+\rho r(x)\) whenever \(\rho>L\kappa\); without a local error bound of this form, no finite exact-penalty threshold follows in general.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local Lipschitz-error-bound boundary for scalar exact penalties.

source_refs.locator: 5.4.3 Linear Suboptimality for Minimization Problems p. 125
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S=\{x:r(x)=0\}\), and suppose \(\bar x\in S\) locally minimizes \(f\). If \(|f(x)-f(z)|\leq L\|x-z\|\) near \(\bar x\) and \(d(x,S)\leq\kappa r(x)\) locally, then every \(\rho>L\kappa\) makes \(\bar x\) a local minimizer of \(P_\rho(x)=f(x)+\rho r(x)\). Thus Lipschitz growth combined with a linear feasibility error bound yields finite exactness. If such an error bound fails, arbitrarily small infeasibility may dominate every fixed linear penalty, so finite exactness is not guaranteed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Lipschitz objective and linear feasibility error bound give exact penalization above a computable threshold; without the error bound, finite exactness may fail.
knowledge_statements.title: Penalty-Exactness Boundaries

source_witnesses.locator: 5.4.3 Linear Suboptimality for Minimization Problems p. 125
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation II

children.title: Smooth Nonlinear Programming Forms
children.top_down_role: Classical equality and inequality constrained forms.

assumptions_latex: \(f,h_j,g_i:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) are continuously differentiable near \(\bar x\).
\(\bar x\) is a local minimizer subject to \(h_j(x)=0\) and \(g_i(x)\leq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exist nonzero Fritz John multipliers satisfying stationarity, sign, and complementarity conditions.

notation.meaning: active inequality indices at the minimizer

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional smooth equality-and-inequality Fritz John rule.

source_refs.locator: 5.1 Necessary Conditions in Mathematical Programming p. 3
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the problem \(\min f(x)\) subject to \(h_j(x)=0\), \(j=1,\ldots,p\), and \(g_i(x)\leq0\), \(i=1,\ldots,m\), let \( ar x\) be a local minimizer. Then there exist \(\lambda_0\geq0\), \(\mu\in\mathbb R^p\), and \(\lambda\in\mathbb R_+^m\), not all zero, such that \[\lambda_0
abla f( ar x)+\sum_{j=1}^p\mu_j
abla h_j( ar x)+\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i
abla g_i( ar x)=0,\qquad \lambda_i g_i( ar x)=0\quad(i=1,\ldots,m).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every smooth constrained local minimizer admits nontrivial Fritz John multipliers satisfying stationarity, nonnegativity, and complementary slackness.
knowledge_statements.title: Smooth Nonlinear Programming Forms

children.title: Geometric Fritz John Forms
children.top_down_role: Multiplier rules expressed through feasible-set geometry.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) and \(F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^q\) are continuously differentiable near \(\bar x\).
\(C\subset\mathbb R^q\) is closed, and \(\bar x\) locally minimizes \(f\) subject to \(F(x)\in C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There are \(\lambda_0\geq0\) and \(y^*\in N_C(F(\bar x))\), not both zero, satisfying \(\lambda_0\nabla f(\bar x)+DF(\bar x)^*y^*=0\).

notation.meaning: limiting normal cone to the closed constraint set
adjoint derivative of the constraint mapping

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional geometric constraint form using limiting normals.

source_refs.locator: 5.1.1 Minimization Problems with Geometric Constraints p. 4
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min f(x)\) subject to \(F(x)\in C\), and let \(\bar x\) be a local minimizer. Under the finite-dimensional geometric extremal rule applicable to this smooth inverse-image system, there exist \(\lambda_0\geq0\) and \(y^*\in N_C(F(\bar x))\), not both zero, such that \[\lambda_0\nabla f(\bar x)+DF(\bar x)^*y^*=0.\] The case \(\lambda_0>0\) is normal and can be scaled to \(\lambda_0=1\); the case \(\lambda_0=0\) is abnormal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A geometric constraint yields an objective multiplier and a normal to the target set whose derivative pullback balances the objective gradient.
knowledge_statements.title: Geometric Fritz John Forms

source_witnesses.locator: 5.1.1 Minimization Problems with Geometric Constraints p. 4
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation II

children.title: Conic Fritz John Forms
children.top_down_role: Multiplier rules for cone-valued constraint systems.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) and \(G:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^q\) are continuously differentiable near \(\bar x\).
\(K\subset\mathbb R^q\) is a closed convex cone, and \(\bar x\) locally minimizes \(f\) subject to \(G(x)\in K\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exist \(\lambda_0\geq0\) and \(y^*\in K^\circ\), not both zero, with stationarity and cone complementarity.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed-convex-cone specialization with negative-polar multipliers.

source_refs.locator: 5.1.1 Minimization Problems with Geometric Constraints p. 4
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\min f(x)\) subject to \(G(x)\in K\), let \(\bar x\) be a local minimizer. The conic Fritz John system consists of \(\lambda_0\geq0\) and \(y^*\in K^\circ\), not both zero, satisfying \[\lambda_0\nabla f(\bar x)+DG(\bar x)^*y^*=0,\qquad \langle y^*,G(\bar x)\rangle=0.\] Equivalently, \(y^*\in N_K(G(\bar x))\). This formulation fixes the negative-polar convention; using the positive dual cone reverses the sign of the multiplier term.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex conic constraint, Fritz John stationarity uses a polar-cone multiplier orthogonal to the feasible cone value.

knowledge_statements.title: Normal-Cone Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth finite-dimensional normal-cone formula under MFCQ.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Gamma=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:h_j(x)=0,\ j=1,\ldots,p,\ g_i(x)\leq0,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\), where every \(h_j\) and \(g_i\) is continuously differentiable near \(\bar x\in\Gamma\). If MFCQ holds at \(\bar x\), then \[N_\Gamma(\bar x)=\left\{\sum_{j=1}^p\mu_j\nabla h_j(\bar x)+\sum_{i\in I(\bar x)}\lambda_i\nabla g_i(\bar x):\mu\in\mathbb R^p,\ \lambda_i\geq0\right\},\] where \(I(\bar x)=\{i:g_i(\bar x)=0\}\) and \(N_\Gamma\) is the limiting normal cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under MFCQ, the limiting normal cone to the smooth feasible set consists exactly of equality-gradient combinations plus nonnegative combinations of active inequality gradients.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the negative polar \(K^\circ=\{z:\langle z,k\rangle\leq0\text{ for every }k\in K\}\), the normal cone to a closed convex cone satisfies \[N_K(y)=\{z\in K^\circ:\langle z,y\rangle=0\}=K^\circ\cap y^\perp\qquad(y\in K).\] Consequently, membership of a conic multiplier in \(N_K(y)\) is equivalent to dual feasibility \(z\in K^\circ\) together with complementarity \(\langle z,y\rangle=0\). Under the positive-dual convention, the corresponding multiplier is \(-z\).

children.title: Normal Multiplier Regimes

knowledge_statements.title: Normal Multiplier Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive-objective-multiplier branch of smooth Fritz John systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider \(\min f(x)\) subject to \(h_j(x)=0\), \(j=1,\ldots,p\), and \(g_i(x)\leq0\), \(i=1,\ldots,m\), where the functions are continuously differentiable near the feasible point \( ar x\). A nonzero Fritz John multiplier tuple \((\lambda_0,\mu,\lambda)\) is normal when \(\lambda_0>0\). Its normalized multipliers \(\widehat\mu=\mu/\lambda_0\) and \(\widehat\lambda=\lambda/\lambda_0\) satisfy \[
abla f( ar x)+\sum_{j=1}^p\widehat\mu_j
abla h_j( ar x)+\sum_{i=1}^m\widehat\lambda_i
abla g_i( ar x)=0,\qquad \widehat\lambda_i\geq0,\qquad \widehat\lambda_i g_i( ar x)=0.\] Thus every normal Fritz John tuple determines a KKT tuple.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Fritz John tuple with positive objective multiplier can be divided by that multiplier to obtain KKT multipliers with objective multiplier one.
assumptions_latex: \(f,h_j,g_i:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) are continuously differentiable near a feasible point \(\bar x\).
\((\lambda_0,\mu,\lambda)\) is a nonzero Fritz John multiplier tuple at \(\bar x\) with \(\lambda_0>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The normalized tuple \(\left(1,\mu/\lambda_0,\lambda/\lambda_0\right)\) satisfies the KKT stationarity, sign, and complementarity conditions.

knowledge_statements.title: Abnormal Multiplier Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Zero-objective-multiplier branch marking failure of KKT normalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider \(\min f(x)\) subject to \(h_j(x)=0\), \(j=1,\ldots,p\), and \(g_i(x)\leq0\), \(i=1,\ldots,m\), where the functions are continuously differentiable near the feasible point \( ar x\). A nonzero Fritz John tuple \((\lambda_0,\mu,\lambda)\) is abnormal when \(\lambda_0=0\). It then satisfies \[\sum_{j=1}^p\mu_j
abla h_j( ar x)+\sum_{i\in I( ar x)}\lambda_i
abla g_i( ar x)=0,\qquad \lambda_i\geq0,\qquad (\mu,\lambda)
eq0,\] where \(I( ar x)=\{i:g_i( ar x)=0\}\). No positive scaling of this tuple can produce an objective multiplier equal to \(1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An abnormal Fritz John tuple has zero objective multiplier and a nontrivial homogeneous dependence among equality and active-inequality gradients, so it cannot be normalized to a KKT tuple.
assumptions_latex: \(f,h_j,g_i:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) are continuously differentiable near a feasible point \(\bar x\).
\((0,\mu,\lambda)\) is a nonzero Fritz John multiplier tuple at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The constraint multipliers satisfy a nontrivial homogeneous active-gradient relation, and no positive scaling yields objective multiplier \(1\).

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The rescaling \((\lambda_0,\mu,\lambda)\mapsto(1,\mu/\lambda_0,\lambda/\lambda_0)\) preserves feasibility, stationarity, and complementarity.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Homogeneous rescaling from Fritz John to KKT multipliers.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \((\lambda_0,\mu,\lambda)\) satisfies the Fritz John equations, then \((t\lambda_0,t\mu,t\lambda)\) satisfies them for every \(t>0\). When \(\lambda_0>0\), choosing \(t=1/\lambda_0\) produces the equivalent normalized tuple \[(1,\widehat\mu,\widehat\lambda)=\left(1,\frac{\mu}{\lambda_0},\frac{\lambda}{\lambda_0}\right).\] Sign restrictions and complementary slackness are invariant under this positive scaling. When \(\lambda_0=0\), no positive scaling reaches the normalized hyperplane \(\lambda_0=1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive homogeneity permits transition from a normal Fritz John tuple to a KKT tuple, while the abnormal branch cannot cross to objective multiplier one.

knowledge_statements.title: Qualification-Controlled Normality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: MFCQ exclusion of abnormal smooth nonlinear-programming multipliers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min f(x)\) subject to \(h_j(x)=0\), \(j=1,\ldots,p\), and \(g_i(x)\leq0\), \(i=1,\ldots,m\), where the functions are continuously differentiable near a feasible point \(\bar x\). If MFCQ holds at \(\bar x\), then every nonzero Fritz John multiplier tuple \((\lambda_0,\mu,\lambda)\) at \(\bar x\) satisfies \(\lambda_0>0\). Consequently, every such tuple can be positively rescaled to a KKT tuple with objective multiplier \(1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a smooth equality-and-inequality constrained problem, MFCQ excludes nonzero abnormal Fritz John multipliers and therefore permits KKT normalization.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At a feasible point \( ar x\), the Mangasarian–Fromovitz constraint qualification holds if the equality gradients \(\{
abla h_j( ar x)\}_{j=1}^p\) are linearly independent and there exists \(d\in\mathbb R^n\) such that \[
abla h_j( ar x)^Td=0\quad(j=1,\ldots,p),\qquad 
abla g_i( ar x)^Td<0\quad(i\in I( ar x)).\] Equivalently, no nonzero pair \((\mu,\lambda)\), with \(\lambda_i\geq0\) on active indices, satisfies the homogeneous active-gradient stationarity relation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: MFCQ combines independent equality gradients with a direction tangent to all equalities and strictly decreasing every active inequality.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Dimensional Convex Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical finite-valued convex inequalities with affine equalities in Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For convex finite-valued functions \(g_i:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\), \(i=1,\ldots,m\), a linear map \(A:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^p\), and \(b\in\mathbb{R}^p\), the finite-dimensional Slater condition for \[g_i(x)\le0\quad(i=1,\ldots,m),\qquad Ax=b\] holds if there exists \(x^s\in\mathbb{R}^n\) such that \[Ax^s=b,\qquad g_i(x^s)<0\quad(i=1,\ldots,m).\]

knowledge_statements.title: Conic Slater Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine conic feasibility with a solid closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be finite-dimensional real vector spaces, let \(K\subset Y\) be a closed convex cone with nonempty interior, let \(A:X\to Y\) be linear, and let \(b\in Y\). For the affine conic system \[b-Ax\in K,\] the conic Slater condition holds if there exists \(x^s\in X\) such that \[b-Ax^s\in\operatorname{int}K.\] Equivalently, \((b-A(X))\cap\operatorname{int}K\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Conic Slater qualification requires a feasible point whose affine conic slack lies in the topological interior of the cone.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are finite-dimensional real vector spaces.
\(K\subset Y\) is a closed convex cone with nonempty interior.
\(A:X\to Y\) is linear and \(b\in Y\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The algebraic interior, or core, of \(C\) is \[\operatorname{core}C=\{x\in C:\forall d\in X\ \exists\varepsilon_d>0\ \forall |t|<\varepsilon_d,\ x+td\in C\}.\] A core qualification for the pair of convex constraints \(x\in C\) and \(x\in D\) is \[\operatorname{core}C\cap D\ne\varnothing.\] Thus one constraint set contains a feasible point admitting sufficiently short displacements in every algebraic direction.

notation.meaning: Strong quasi-relative interior of a convex set.
Minkowski difference of the constraint sets.
Conical hull based at a point.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong quasi-relative-interior difference qualification in a locally convex space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a convex set \(S\subset X\), define \[\operatorname{sqri}S=\{x\in S:\operatorname{cone}(S-x)\ \text{is a closed linear subspace of }X\}.\] An infinite-dimensional interior-surrogate qualification for the pair \(C,D\) is \[0\in\operatorname{sqri}(C-D).\] This condition substitutes a closed linearity property of the generated cone for nonempty topological interior, which frequently fails in function spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An infinite-dimensional surrogate qualification places zero in the strong quasi-relative interior of the difference of two convex constraint sets.
knowledge_statements.title: Infinite-Dimensional Interior Surrogates

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The sqri definition and difference condition are plausible, but an authoritative source is required to confirm the exact locally convex-space hypotheses and that this is the intended interior-surrogate qualification.

children.title: Constant-Rank Qualifications
children.top_down_role: Rank-stability regimes for active constraints.

assumptions_latex: \(g_i,h_j:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) are continuously differentiable near a feasible point \(\bar x\).
\(I(\bar x)=\{i:g_i(\bar x)=0\}\) is the active inequality index set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every family \(\{\nabla h_j(x):j=1,\ldots,p\}\cup\{\nabla g_i(x):i\in J\}\) has constant rank near \(\bar x\), for each \(J\subset I(\bar x)\).

notation.meaning: Active inequality indices at the reference point.
An arbitrary subset of active inequality indices.
Constraint-gradient matrix for the selected family.

source_refs.locator: 3.2 Constraint Qualifications p. 252

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each subset \(J\subset I(\bar x)\), let \(M_J(x)\) have columns \(\nabla h_j(x)\), \(j=1,\ldots,p\), and \(\nabla g_i(x)\), \(i\in J\). The constant-rank constraint qualification holds at \(\bar x\) if there is a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\) such that, for every \(J\subset I(\bar x)\), \[\operatorname{rank}M_J(x)=\operatorname{rank}M_J(\bar x)\qquad\text{for all }x\in U.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Constant-rank qualification requires every family formed from equality gradients and any subset of active inequality gradients to retain its rank nearby.

children.title: Robinson Constraint Qualification
children.top_down_role: Conic and generalized-equation regularity regime.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are Banach spaces, \(F:X\to Y\) is continuously Fréchet differentiable near \(\bar x\), and \(D\subset Y\) is closed and convex.
The reference point is feasible: \(F(\bar x)\in D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\in\operatorname{int}\bigl(F(\bar x)+F'(\bar x)X-D\bigr)\).

notation.meaning: Fréchet derivative of the constraint mapping at the reference point.
Topological interior in the range space.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Banach-space smooth mapping constrained to a closed convex set.

source_refs.locator: 4.3.2 Lipschitzian Stability of Constraint Systems p. 414
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the constraint system \(F(x)\in D\), Robinson constraint qualification holds at the feasible point \(\bar x\) when \[0\in\operatorname{int}\bigl(F(\bar x)+F'(\bar x)X-D\bigr).\] Equivalently, the linearized displacement mapping \(d\mapsto F(\bar x)+F'(\bar x)d-D\) covers a neighborhood of the origin in \(Y\). The interior is taken in the norm topology of the range space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Robinson qualification requires the linearized constraint-displacement set to contain a neighborhood of zero in the range space.

children.title: Metric Regularity Qualifications
children.top_down_role: Openness and inverse-stability regimes for constraint mappings.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are metric spaces, and \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\).
\((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) satisfies a locally uniform inverse-stability estimate around \((\bar x,\bar y)\).

notation.meaning: Distance from a point to a set, with value infinity for the empty set.
Inverse image of a point under a set-valued mapping.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local metric-space definition at a graph point.

source_refs.locator: 1.2.3 Metric Regularity and Covering p. 56
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The mapping \(F\) is metrically regular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) if there exist neighborhoods \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and \(V\) of \(\bar y\), and a constant \(\kappa\geq 0\), such that
\[
d(x,F^{-1}(y))\leq \kappa\,d(y,F(x))\qquad\text{for every }(x,y)\in U\times V.
\]
The infimum of all admissible \(\kappa\) is the exact regularity modulus \(\operatorname{reg}F(\bar x\mid\bar y)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Metric regularity bounds the distance to every nearby inverse image by the corresponding mapping residual, uniformly in both the decision and perturbation variables.
knowledge_statements.title: Metric Regularity Qualifications

source_witnesses.locator: 1.2.3 Metric Regularity and Covering p. 56
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

children.title: Metric Subregularity Qualifications
children.top_down_role: Localized residual-control regimes.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are metric spaces, and \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\).
\((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d(x,F^{-1}(\bar y))\leq\kappa d(\bar y,F(x))\) holds locally in \(x\).

notation.meaning: Solution set for the fixed target value.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-target residual qualification, local only in the decision variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The mapping \(F\) is metrically subregular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) if there exist a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and \(\kappa\geq0\) such that
\[
d(x,F^{-1}(\bar y))\leq \kappa\,d(\bar y,F(x))\qquad\text{for every }x\in U.
\]
The infimum of the admissible constants is denoted by \(\operatorname{subreg}F(\bar x\mid\bar y)\). Unlike metric regularity, the comparison value is fixed at \(\bar y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Metric subregularity locally controls distance to the fixed solution set by the residual at the fixed target value.
knowledge_statements.title: Metric Subregularity Qualifications

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The fixed-target inequality is the standard metric-subregularity definition and the definition content kind fits the leaf, but the record supplies no source or inspectable locator. Source support is required before candidate-review acceptance.

children.top_down_role: Perturbation and residual formulations of weaker regularity.

children.title: Calmness Qualifications
children.top_down_role: One-sided stability conditions for perturbed solution mappings.

assumptions_latex: \(P\) and \(X\) are metric spaces, and \(S:P\rightrightarrows X\).
\((\bar p,\bar x)\in\operatorname{gph}S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Nearby values of \(S(p)\) cannot depart from \(S(\bar p)\) faster than linearly in \(d(p,\bar p)\).

notation.meaning: Excess of one set over another.
Closed ball centered at the reference solution.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise calmness of a set-valued solution mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The mapping \(S\) is calm at \((\bar p,\bar x)\) if there exist neighborhoods \(V\) of \(\bar p\) and \(U\) of \(\bar x\), and \(L\geq0\), such that
\[
d(x,S(\bar p))\leq L\,d(p,\bar p)
\]
for every \(p\in V\) and every \(x\in S(p)\cap U\). Equivalently, after shrinking \(U\), one has \(e(S(p)\cap U,S(\bar p))\leq Ld(p,\bar p)\) for all \(p\in V\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Calmness gives a one-sided Lipschitz bound on nearby solutions relative to the solution set at the reference parameter.
knowledge_statements.title: Calmness Qualifications

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated pointwise calmness condition is standard and fits the calmness qualification leaf, but no source or locator is supplied. The claimed excess-form equivalence also requires authoritative support.

children.title: Error-Bound Qualifications
children.top_down_role: Residual-based control of local feasibility.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are metric spaces, and \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\).
\((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The residual \(d(\bar y,F(x))\) locally bounds the distance to the feasible set \(F^{-1}(\bar y)\).

notation.meaning: Feasible set associated with the target value.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local linear error bound for a set-valued constraint system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The constraint \(\bar y\in F(x)\) has a local error bound at \(\bar x\) if there exist a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and \(\kappa\geq0\) such that
\[
d(x,\Omega)\leq\kappa r(x)\qquad\text{for all }x\in U,
\]
where \(\Omega=F^{-1}(\bar y)\) and \(r(x)=d(\bar y,F(x))\). Thus this qualification is precisely metric subregularity of \(F\) at \((\bar x,\bar y)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A local error bound estimates distance to feasibility by a computable constraint residual; it is metric subregularity in residual form.
knowledge_statements.title: Error-Bound Qualifications

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The local error-bound condition is consistent with metric subregularity for the specified residual and the condition content kind fits the container. No source or inspectable locator supports the equivalence, however.

children.title: Perturbation–Residual Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Links between mapping stability and feasibility residual estimates.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are metric spaces, and \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\).
\((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is metrically subregular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) if and only if \(F^{-1}\) is calm at \((\bar y,\bar x)\), with equal exact moduli.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Inverse-mapping equivalence between fixed-target residual control and perturbation stability.

source_refs.locator: 4.1.2 Neighborhood Characterizations of Metric Regularity and Lipschitzian Behavior p. 382
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(S=F^{-1}\). Then \(F\) is metrically subregular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) if and only if \(S\) is calm at \((\bar y,\bar x)\). Indeed, the two defining inequalities are the same after observing that
\[
d(x,S(\bar y))=d(x,F^{-1}(\bar y))
\]
and that \(x\in S(y)\) is equivalent to \(y\in F(x)\). Consequently,
\[
\operatorname{subreg}F(\bar x\mid\bar y)=\operatorname{clm}F^{-1}(\bar y\mid\bar x).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Metric subregularity of a constraint mapping is exactly calmness of its inverse solution mapping, and their best constants coincide.
knowledge_statements.title: Perturbation–Residual Correspondence

source_witnesses.locator: 4.1.2 Neighborhood Characterizations of Metric Regularity and Lipschitzian Behavior p. 382
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The subregularity-calmness equivalence and equality of exact moduli are standard, and duality is an appropriate content kind. However, the cited locator is titled for metric regularity and Lipschitzian behavior rather than the pointwise subregularity-calmness correspondence, so support for this exact claim is uncertain. The sentences beginning with “Indeed” also present proof-style derivation that must be removed after an appropriate source is supplied.

children.title: Weak-Regularity Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Separations from metric subregularity or stronger mapping properties.

assumptions_latex: \(F:\mathbb R\rightrightarrows\mathbb R\) is defined by \(F(x)=\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is metrically subregular but not metrically regular at \((0,0)\); equivalently, \(F^{-1}\) is calm but lacks the Aubin property there.

notation.meaning: Inverse mapping of the constant mapping.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete separation of weak and uniform mapping regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(F(x)=\{0\}\), one has \(F^{-1}(0)=\mathbb R\), so
\[
d(x,F^{-1}(0))=0\leq\kappa d(0,F(x))
\]
for every \(x\) and every \(\kappa\geq0\); hence \(F\) is metrically subregular at \((0,0)\). It is not metrically regular there because every neighborhood of \(0\) contains \(y\ne0\), while \(F^{-1}(y)=\varnothing\), making \(d(x,F^{-1}(y))=+\infty\). Thus fixed-target residual control does not imply uniform perturbation stability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The constant zero mapping is subregular but not regular, showing that fixed-target control does not guarantee stability for nearby target perturbations.
knowledge_statements.title: Weak-Regularity Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The constant-zero mapping is a valid separation example and failure_boundary is the correct role for this leaf. The record has no source, and its statement includes an extended proof-style verification rather than a concise sourced counterexample statement.
